category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A mutation involving the replacement of a single nucleotide base with another, which can result in a silent, missense, or nonsense effect, is termed a [___].
back:
* Point mutation
* Involves single base substitution
* Results depend on the degeneracy of the genetic code.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A neonate presents with phenotypic features of Down syndrome. Karyotype analysis reveals 46 chromosomes, with one chromosome 14 carrying the long arm of chromosome 21. Name the specific structural abnormality.
back:
* Robertsonian Translocation
* Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes
* Results in a balanced carrier or unbalanced phenotype.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain how a frameshift mutation typically affects the translation of a protein compared to a point mutation.
back:
* Alters the reading frame by inserting/deleting bases (not multiples of three)
* Changes all subsequent amino acids
* Frequently creates premature stop codons.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient with Turner Syndrome (45,X) presents with a milder phenotype than expected. Analysis shows 45,X in blood cells but 46,XX in skin cells. Contrast this condition's origin with standard nondisjunction.
back:
* Mosaicism results from mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization
* Standard nondisjunction occurs during gametogenesis (meiosis)
* Mosaics possess multiple cell lines with distinct genotypes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the chromosomal mutation where a DNA segment is removed and reinserted in the reverse orientation within the same chromosome.
back:
* Inversion
* Pericentric involves the centromere; Paracentric does not
* Usually balanced in the carrier but can produce unbalanced gametes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The loss of a DNA segment, which can range from a single nucleotide to an entire chromosome arm, is classified as a [___].
back:
* Deletion
* Leads to loss of genetic material
* Example: 5p deletion in Cri-du-chat syndrome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: An infant is born with multiple congenital anomalies. Genetic testing confirms an 'Insertion' mutation in a regulatory gene. Explain the potential downstream effect on the resulting protein.
back:
* Addition of nucleotides disrupts the triplet code
* May cause a frameshift or insert extra amino acids
* Often results in a non-functional or unstable protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the biochemical consequences of a nonsense point mutation occurring early in a coding sequence.
back:
* Substitution creates a stop codon (UAG, UAA, or UGA)
* Results in premature termination of translation
* Produces a truncated, likely non-functional protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between a silent mutation and a missense mutation regarding their impact on the final amino acid sequence.
back:
* Silent: No change in amino acid due to code redundancy
* Missense: One amino acid is replaced by a different one
* Both result from single-base substitutions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: State the standard total chromosome count in a balanced Robertsonian Translocation carrier.
back:
* 45 chromosomes
* Two acrocentric chromosomes are fused into one
* Genetic material is effectively normal despite the lower count.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A single nucleotide substitution that replaces a sense codon with a stop codon is specifically called a [___] mutation.
back:
Nonsense mutation

* Results in premature termination of translation.
* Produces a truncated, usually non-functional polypeptide.
* May trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay pathways.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient is found to have a 1-base pair insertion in a gene coding for a lysosomal enzyme, resulting in an entirely different amino acid sequence downstream. This is a [___].
back:
Frameshift mutation

* Caused by insertions or deletions not divisible by three.
* Shifts the triplet reading frame of mRNA.
* Often introduces a premature stop codon further downstream.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism of a Robertsonian Translocation involving acrocentric chromosomes.
back:
Mechanism:

* Fusion of the long arms (q) of two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21).
* Loss of the short arms (p), which contain redundant rRNA genes.
* Reduces total chromosome count to 45 in balanced carriers.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the structural effect of a pericentric inversion with a paracentric inversion.
back:
Differential Contrast:

* Pericentric: Involves the centromere; can change the arm length ratio (p/q).
* Paracentric: Excludes the centromere; occurs within a single arm.
* Both are balanced rearrangements but increase risk of unbalanced gametes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the cellular origin of mosaicism in an individual with chromosomal abnormalities.
back:
Conceptual Basis:

* Occurs due to mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization.
* Results in two or more genetically distinct cell lines within one person.
* Phenotypic severity often depends on the percentage of affected cells.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The loss of a segment of DNA without shifting the reading frame, such as the three-base loss in the CFTR ΔF508 mutation, is an in-frame [___].
back:
Deletion

* Removes one or more amino acids from the protein.
* Reading frame remains intact if the loss is a multiple of three.
* Leads to protein misfolding or functional loss.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 25-year-old male presents with sickle cell anemia. The underlying mutation is a single base substitution (GAG to GTG). Classify this mutation type.
back:
Missense Mutation

* A point mutation resulting in a different amino acid (Glutamate to Valine).
* This specific case is a transversion (A to T).
* Changes protein conformation and stability (HbS polymerization).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: How does an insertion of two nucleotides into the middle of an exon affect the resulting protein product?
back:
Mechanism:

* Induces a frameshift, altering every subsequent codon.
* Typically results in a radically altered primary sequence.
* Most insertions eventually lead to a premature stop codon and truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Compare the genetic consequences of a balanced translocation vs. an unbalanced translocation in a fetus.
back:
Metabolic/Physiological Contrast:

* Balanced: No gain or loss of genetic material; usually phenotypically normal.
* Unbalanced: Significant deletion or duplication of genes; usually results in severe malformations or lethality.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Differentiate between transition and transversion in point mutations.
back:
Biochemical Fact:

* Transition: Substitution of a purine for a purine (A↔G) or pyrimidine for pyrimidine (C↔T).
* Transversion: Substitution of a purine for a pyrimidine or vice versa.
* Transitions occur more frequently in the genome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
coreConcept: Point Mutation in Sickle Cell Anemia
front: In sickle cell anemia, a point mutation in the beta-globin gene causes the GAG codon to become [___], resulting in valine replacing glutamate.
back:
• The answer is GTG.
• This represents a missense mutation.
• It alters the physical properties of hemoglobin, causing polymerization under deoxygenated conditions in the RBC.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 4-year-old child presents with recurrent pulmonary infections and salty sweat. Genetic testing reveals a 3-base pair deletion at position 508. Describe the effect on the resulting protein.
back:
• Loss of a phenylalanine residue (ΔF508).
• Leads to improper protein folding in the RER.
• The CFTR protein is ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome before reaching the membrane.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism by which a 1-base pair insertion leads to a non-functional protein product.
back:
• Causes a frameshift mutation.
• This shifts the triplet reading frame of mRNA.
• Results in an entirely different amino acid sequence downstream and often creates a premature stop codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast a silent point mutation with a nonsense point mutation regarding their effects on the polypeptide chain.
back:
• Silent: No change in amino acid sequence due to genetic code degeneracy.
• Nonsense: Creates a premature stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA).
• Result: Leads to a truncated, usually non-functional protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the structural consequence of a chromosomal inversion on a DNA segment.
back:
• A segment of DNA is broken in two places.
• The segment is reversed 180 degrees and reattached.
• May disrupt gene expression if breaks occur in coding or regulatory regions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A translocation involving the fusion of long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with the loss of their short arms is specifically termed a [___].
back:
• Robertsonian Translocation.
• Involves chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22.
• Clinically significant for causing translocational Down Syndrome in offspring.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A child exhibits mild features of Down Syndrome. Karyotyping shows some cells with 46 chromosomes and others with 47. Explain the likely developmental cause.
back:
• Nondisjunction occurring post-fertilization during mitosis.
• Results in mosaicism.
• The individual has two distinct cell populations with different genotypes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: How does trinucleotide repeat expansion in the Huntington (HTT) gene lead to neurodegeneration?
back:
• CAG repeats expand beyond the normal threshold.
• Produces an abnormally long polyglutamine tract.
• The mutant protein is cleaved into toxic fragments that aggregate in neurons, causing cell death.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between a 3-bp deletion and a 1-bp deletion in a coding region.
back:
• 3-bp deletion: Removes exactly one amino acid; the reading frame remains intact.
• 1-bp deletion: Causes a frameshift mutation.
• Result: Alters all subsequent codons, usually creating a premature termination signal.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Determine the effect of a mutation that changes a sense codon to a stop codon.
back:
• This is a nonsense mutation.
• It prematurely terminates translation.
• Produces a shortened protein fragment which is typically degraded or lacks biological activity.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that converts a sense codon into a premature termination signal, resulting in a truncated protein product, is known as a [___] mutation.
back: Nonsense mutation. Leads to premature chain termination. Often results in non-functional proteins.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A genetic analysis of a patient with Duchenne muscular dystrophy reveals a single nucleotide insertion within an exon. Explain the most likely effect on the resulting polypeptide chain.
back: Frameshift mutation. It alters the reading frame of the mRNA. Results in a radically different amino acid sequence or premature stop.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the role of the acrocentric chromosomes during the formation of a Robertsonian Translocation.
back: Fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21). The long arms join at a centromere. The short arms are typically lost.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the structural genomic consequences of a chromosomal deletion versus a balanced inversion.
back: Deletion: Loss of a DNA segment; reduced genetic material. Inversion: Segment is reversed 180 degrees; no loss of material; only rearrangement occurs.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the physiological outcome of a silent mutation at the third position of a codon.
back: No change in the amino acid sequence. Occurs due to the degeneracy of the genetic code. Protein function remains unaffected.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The presence of two or more genetically distinct cell lines derived from a single zygote due to post-zygotic mitotic errors is termed [___].
back: Mosaicism. Caused by nondisjunction in early development. Leads to varying clinical severity of genetic syndromes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient presents with symptoms of Huntington disease. Genetic testing confirms an expansion of CAG repeats. Identify the mutation type and its effect on the protein structure.
back: Trinucleotide repeat expansion. Results in extra glutamine residues. Causes protein aggregation and neurotoxicity.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: How does the insertion of exactly three nucleotides into a coding sequence differ from the insertion of one nucleotide in terms of the reading frame?
back: Three nucleotides: In-frame insertion; adds one amino acid. One nucleotide: Frameshift mutation; shifts the entire downstream reading frame.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between pericentric and paracentric inversions.
back: Pericentric: Involves the centromere; break points on both arms. Paracentric: Does not involve the centromere; break points on a single arm.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the primary mechanism behind the production of Hemoglobin S in sickle cell anemia.
back: Missense point mutation. Glutamate is replaced by Valine at position 6. Alters the hemoglobin tetramer structure.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that results in the conversion of a sense codon into a premature termination codon is specifically termed a [___] mutation.
back:
* Nonsense mutation
* Results in a truncated, often non-functional protein
* Commonly leads to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay pathways.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 5-year-old male presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness and Gower's sign. Genetic analysis reveals a deletion in the dystrophin gene that is not a multiple of three. Identify the specific mutation category and its effect.
back:
* Frameshift mutation
* Alters the entire downstream reading frame
* Usually results in a premature stop codon and complete loss of functional protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the role of acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) in the mechanism of a Robertsonian Translocation.
back:
* Fusion of the long arms (q) of two acrocentric chromosomes
* Loss of the short arms (p) containing redundant rRNA genes
* Results in a balanced carrier with 45 chromosomes but a normal phenotype.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the clinical severity of Down Syndrome caused by meiotic nondisjunction with that caused by mitotic nondisjunction occurring after fertilization.
back:
* Meiotic: All cells possess Trisomy 21; typically presents with the full clinical phenotype.
* Mitotic (Mosaicism): Only a percentage of cell lines are affected.
* Outcome: Mosaicism generally presents with milder physical and intellectual features.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Why does a single nucleotide deletion in an exon typically cause more severe metabolic disruption than a three-nucleotide deletion?
back:
* Single deletion: Causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation.
* Triple deletion: Removes exactly one amino acid (in-frame), preserving the rest of the sequence.
* Consequence: Frameshifts frequently create early stop codons.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A chromosomal mutation characterized by a 180-degree reversal of a DNA segment that includes the centromere is termed a [___] inversion.
back:
* Pericentric inversion
* Includes the centromere within the inverted segment
* Can alter the relative lengths of the p and q arms of the chromosome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient with Sickle Cell Anemia has a single base substitution (Adenine to Thymine) in the β-globin gene. Apply the correct terminology for this mutation and its biochemical result.
back:
* Missense mutation (specifically a Transversion)
* Glutamic acid is replaced by Valine at position 6
* Result: Creates a hydrophobic patch leading to hemoglobin polymerization.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between a 'Balanced' and 'Unbalanced' translocation in terms of genetic content and clinical impact on offspring.
back:
* Balanced: No net loss/gain of DNA; carrier is usually healthy.
* Unbalanced: Net loss or gain of genetic material (monosomy/trisomy segments).
* Impact: Unbalanced translocations lead to spontaneous abortion or severe congenital malformations.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Compare the molecular composition change in a Transition versus a Transversion point mutation.
back:
* Transition: Purine replaced by Purine (A to G) or Pyrimidine by Pyrimidine (C to T).
* Transversion: Purine replaced by a Pyrimidine (e.g., A to C) or vice versa.
* Frequency: Transitions are more common in human genetics.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the chromosomal mutation that results in the gain of a DNA segment, often leading to gene dosage effects or over-expression.
back:
* Insertion (or Duplication)
* Adds extra copies of genetic material to a chromosome
* Consequence: May disrupt existing genes at the insertion site or cause toxic protein levels.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that replaces a sense codon with a termination signal, leading to the production of a truncated protein, is termed a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation
• Results in premature termination of translation
• Often leads to a non-functional or unstable protein product.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A child presents with a history of recurrent pulmonary infections and sweat tests positive for high chloride. A 3-base deletion (ΔF508) in the CFTR gene is identified. Describe the effect of this mutation on the DNA and protein.
back:
• Loss of a specific amino acid (phenylalanine)
• Reading frame remains intact
• Leads to protein misfolding and subsequent proteasomal degradation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain how a frameshift mutation specifically alters the biological information within a coding segment of DNA.
back:
• Addition or deletion of 1-2 nucleotides
• Changes the entire downstream reading frame
• Produces a radically different amino acid sequence or early stop codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the functional outcomes of a 'silent' mutation versus a 'missense' mutation in the context of protein-coding DNA segments.
back:
• Silent: Nucleotide change results in the same amino acid; protein function is unchanged.
• Missense: Nucleotide change results in a different amino acid; can significantly alter protein function.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the primary structural effect of a chromosomal inversion on a segment of DNA.
back:
• 180-degree rotation of a DNA segment
• Reversal of the internal gene sequence
• Often disrupts gene expression if breakpoints occur within a coding region.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The condition where an individual possesses two or more genetically distinct cell lines originating from a single zygote is called [___].
back:
• Mosaicism
• Results from post-fertilization (mitotic) errors
• Leads to a mixture of normal and mutated cells in the body.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A parent is found to be a carrier of a Robertsonian Translocation involving chromosomes 14 and 21. Describe the structural change to the DNA segments involved.
back:
• Fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes at their centromeres
• Loss of the short (p) arms containing redundant rRNA genes
• Formation of a single, large hybrid chromosome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism by which a splice site mutation results in abnormal protein production as seen in certain thalassemias.
back:
• Mutation at intron-exon junctions
• Leads to improper removal of introns or skipping of exons
• Produces mRNA with abnormal lengths and disrupted coding sequences.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between the effect of an insertion of one nucleotide versus an insertion of three nucleotides within an exon.
back:
• 1-Nucleotide: Causes a frameshift, altering all downstream amino acids.
• 3-Nucleotide: Adds a single amino acid while maintaining the original reading frame.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the fundamental effect of a deletion mutation on a DNA segment's sequence.
back:
• Removal of one or more nucleotide bases
• Can range from a single base to large chromosomal segments
• Typically results in a loss of genetic information.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A [___] mutation involves the insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides not divisible by three, which shifts the entire downstream reading frame of the mRNA.
back:
* Frameshift mutation
* Alters all subsequent amino acids in the polypeptide chain.
* Often creates a premature stop codon, leading to a non-functional or truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 20-year-old male presents with microcytic anemia. Sequencing reveals a point mutation in the β-globin gene (GAG → GTG) at codon 6. Explain the biochemical effect on the protein.
back:
* Missense Mutation
* Replaces Glutamate (polar) with Valine (nonpolar).
* Leads to Hemoglobin S (Sickle Cell Anemia) and polymer formation under deoxygenated conditions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the structural rearrangement that characterizes a chromosomal inversion.
back:
* A segment of a chromosome breaks in two places.
* The segment rotates 180 degrees and reinserts at the original location.
* Balanced if no genetic material is lost; may disrupt genes at breakpoints.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient with Cystic Fibrosis has a 3-bp deletion (ΔF508), while another has a 1-bp insertion. Contrast the expected structural impact on their respective CFTR proteins.
back:
* 3-bp Deletion (ΔF508): Removes one amino acid (Phenylalanine); reading frame is preserved; protein is misfolded but partially translated.
* 1-bp Insertion: Causes a frameshift; shifts entire reading frame; results in non-functional truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the specific point mutation where a base substitution results in the conversion of a sense codon into a termination codon.
back:
* Nonsense Mutation
* Results in premature termination of the polypeptide chain.
* Often leads to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay or production of truncated proteins.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: In conditions like Down Syndrome, [___] is the presence of two genetically distinct cell lines (e.g., 46,XX and 47,XX,+21) within the same individual due to post-zygotic nondisjunction.
back:
* Mosaicism
* Occurs due to mitotic errors after fertilization.
* Typically results in a milder clinical phenotype than full trisomy.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Analysis of a patient with Hemoglobin Constant Spring shows a 172-amino acid β-globin chain instead of the normal 141. Identify the mutation type at the original stop codon.
back:
* Stop-loss mutation (Point mutation)
* Termination codon (e.g., UAA) is mutated to a sense codon.
* Translation continues into the 3'-untranslated region (UTR) until the next stop codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism by which a balanced Robertsonian translocation in a parent leads to a high risk of producing offspring with Trisomy 21.
back:
* Involves fusion of long arms of acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21).
* Adjacent segregation during meiosis produces gametes with disomy.
* Fertilization with a normal gamete results in a zygote with three copies of chromosome 21 material.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the structural genomic outcomes of a paracentric inversion versus a pericentric inversion.
back:
* Paracentric: Inversion occurs within one arm; does not involve the centromere.
* Pericentric: Inversion involves the centromere; can change the length ratio of the p and q arms (arm-ratio change).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the chromosomal mutation characterized by the fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes and the loss of their short arms.
back:
* Robertsonian Translocation
* Only occurs in acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22).
* Carriers have 45 chromosomes but are usually phenotypically normal.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that converts an amino acid-coding codon into a UAA, UAG, or UGA codon is specifically classified as a [___] mutation.
back: * Nonsense mutation. * Results in premature termination of protein synthesis. * Leads to a truncated protein product.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A newborn is screened for an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a three-base pair deletion in the CFTR gene. Explain the effect of this specific deletion on the resulting protein primary structure.
back: * Deletion of one complete codon (phenylalanine 508). * Protein is produced but misfolds and is degraded. * Reading frame remains unaltered.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the mechanism by which a pericentric inversion alters the chromosome structure compared to a paracentric inversion.
back: * Pericentric involves two breaks on opposite sides of the centromere. * Paracentric involves two breaks within the same arm. * Pericentric inversions change the p/q arm ratio.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A phenotypically normal male is found to have 45 chromosomes with one large chromosome formed by the fusion of the q-arms of chromosomes 14 and 21. Contrast this with a reciprocal translocation.
back: * Robertsonian: Fusion of acrocentric chromosomes at centromeres with loss of p-arms. * Reciprocal: Exchange of segments between any two non-homologous chromosomes. * Robertsonian changes the total chromosome count.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Specify the effect on the protein reading frame when an insertion of two nucleotides occurs within a coding exon.
back: * Results in a frameshift mutation. * Every amino acid sequence after the insertion point is changed. * Usually results in a non-functional truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The presence of distinct cell lines, such as some cells having 46 chromosomes and others 47 (Trisomy 21), in a single individual is called [___].
back: * Mosaicism. * Caused by mitotic non-disjunction after zygote formation. * Often results in a milder clinical presentation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient analysis reveals a valine substitution for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain. Identify the specific mutation category and its immediate biological consequence.
back: * Missense point mutation. * Creates a hydrophobic patch on the protein surface. * Leads to hemoglobin polymerization and RBC sickling.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: In the context of the DMD gene, how does a deletion that is not a multiple of three nucleotides impact the muscle cell ability to produce functional dystrophin?
back: * Causes a frameshift mutation. * Leads to a premature stop codon. * Resulting protein is degraded, causing severe muscle weakness.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the molecular impact of a transition point mutation with a transversion point mutation.
back: * Transition: Purine to Purine or Pyrimidine to Pyrimidine. * Transversion: Purine to Pyrimidine or vice versa. * Transitions occur more frequently in the genome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Which specific chromosomal fusion results in the formation of a single chromosome from two acrocentric chromosomes, typically involving chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, or 22?
back: * Robertsonian Translocation. * Results in 45 chromosomes in a balanced carrier. * Involves fusion at the centromeres.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A [___] mutation involves the substitution of a single nucleotide base in the DNA sequence, which may result in silent, missense, or nonsense changes in the encoded protein.
back: Point Mutation. 1) Silent: No amino acid change due to code degeneracy. 2) Missense: Single amino acid substitution. 3) Nonsense: Premature stop codon formation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A neonate is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. The most common mutation, ΔF508, involves the deletion of three nucleotides. Explain the effect of this specific deletion on the reading frame.
back: The reading frame is maintained because exactly three nucleotides (one codon) are removed. It results in the loss of a phenylalanine residue, leading to CFTR protein misfolding and subsequent degradation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the mechanism by which an insertion of two nucleotides into a coding region affects the resulting polypeptide chain.
back: It causes a frameshift mutation. 1) Shifts the triplet reading frame downstream. 2) Alters every subsequent amino acid. 3) Frequently creates a premature termination codon (nonsense effect).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between a Robertsonian Translocation and a chromosomal inversion regarding their structural impact on the genome.
back: 1) Robertsonian: Fusion of long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of short arms. 2) Inversion: A chromosome segment breaks and reattaches in reverse (180-degree) orientation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the biological basis of mosaicism in an individual following fertilization.
back: Mosaicism arises from post-zygotic mitotic nondisjunction or mutations. It results in an individual possessing two or more genetically distinct cell lines originating from a single zygote.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that converts a sense codon into a premature stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) is specifically termed a [___] mutation.
back: Nonsense Mutation. 1) Results in a truncated (shortened) protein. 2) Usually leads to nonfunctional products. 3) May trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay pathways.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A phenotypically normal mother has 45 chromosomes including a 14;21 translocation. What is the risk to her offspring regarding chromosomal numerical abnormalities?
back: The offspring may inherit an unbalanced translocation. This can result in Translocation Down Syndrome, where the child has 46 chromosomes but three copies of chromosome 21 material.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: How does the degeneracy of the genetic code protect a DNA segment against the functional effects of certain point mutations?
back: Degeneracy allows multiple codons to specify one amino acid. A mutation (often in the 3rd base or 'wobble' position) may result in a silent mutation, preserving protein function.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the genomic effects of a microdeletion versus a large-scale chromosomal deletion.
back: 1) Microdeletion: Affects few nucleotides, potentially causing a frameshift. 2) Large-scale: Removes many genes or entire segments, often leading to severe syndromes or embryonic lethality.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Define a missense mutation and provide a classic clinical example involving hemoglobin.
back: A point mutation where a single base change results in a different amino acid. Example: Sickle Cell Anemia (glutamate to valine substitution in the beta-globin chain).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that creates a premature stop codon, leading to a truncated and often non-functional protein, is specifically termed a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation.
• Converts a sense codon into UAA, UAG, or UGA.
• Results in premature termination of polypeptide synthesis during translation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A neonate is diagnosed with cystic fibrosis. Molecular analysis reveals the loss of three nucleotides at position 508 in the CFTR gene. Identify the effect on the reading frame and the resulting protein fate.
back:
• Frame is maintained (3-base deletion).
• Causes loss of phenylalanine (ΔF508).
• Results in protein misfolding and subsequent proteasomal degradation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural mechanism of a Robertsonian Translocation and its effect on total chromosome count.
back:
• Occurs between two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21).
• Long arms fuse at the centromere; short arms are lost.
• Reduces chromosome count to 45 in balanced carriers.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the structural involvement of the centromere in paracentric versus pericentric chromosomal inversions.
back:
• Paracentric: Inversion occurs in one arm; does not include the centromere.
• Pericentric: Inversion involves both arms; includes the centromere.
• Pericentric inversions can change the chromosome's arm ratio.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish the impact of a 1-base insertion from a 3-base insertion on the downstream protein primary structure.
back:
• 1-base: Frameshift mutation altering all subsequent amino acids.
• 3-base: Insertion of one amino acid; reading frame remains intact.
• Frameshifts typically result in premature stop codons.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The condition where an individual possesses two or more genetically different cell lines derived from a single zygote due to post-zygotic mitotic errors is [___].
back:
• Mosaicism.
• Caused by non-disjunction during early mitotic divisions.
• Often results in a milder clinical phenotype of chromosomal disorders (e.g., Down Syndrome).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient presents with chronic anemia and vaso-occlusive crises. Genetic testing shows a GAG to GTG point mutation in the β-globin gene. Explain the biochemical consequence.
back:
• Missense mutation.
• Replaces hydrophilic glutamate with hydrophobic valine.
• Promotes Hemoglobin S polymerization and RBC sickling under deoxygenated conditions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the phenotypic consequence of haploinsufficiency resulting from a large chromosomal deletion.
back:
• Loss of a chromosomal segment reduces gene dosage.
• Single remaining functional allele cannot produce sufficient protein.
• Results in specific malformation syndromes (e.g., Cri-du-chat).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast transition point mutations with transversion point mutations in terms of nitrogenous base categories.
back:
• Transition: Purine to purine (A↔G) or pyrimidine to pyrimidine (C↔T).
• Transversion: Purine to pyrimidine or pyrimidine to purine.
• Transitions are generally more common in the genome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Define a silent mutation and identify the property of the genetic code that permits it.
back:
• Mutation that does not change the amino acid sequence.
• Permitted by the 'Degeneracy' or 'Redundancy' of the genetic code.
• Usually occurs at the third (wobble) position of the codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A [___] mutation involves the substitution of a single nucleotide base for another, which may result in silent, missense, or nonsense consequences.
back:
• Point mutation
• Can be transitions (purine to purine) or transversions (purine to pyrimidine)
• Effects depend on whether the amino acid sequence is altered or terminated prematurely.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 2-year-old is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. Genetic testing reveals a 3-base deletion (ΔF508). Explain why this specific mutation is not classified as a frameshift.
back:
• Deletion of exactly three bases removes one whole codon.
• The downstream triplet reading frame remains unchanged.
• Results in the loss of a single amino acid (phenylalanine) rather than a global sequence shift.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which a frameshift mutation typically leads to a truncated protein product.
back:
• Insertion or deletion of bases (not multiples of three) shifts the reading frame.
• This shift frequently creates a premature stop codon downstream.
• Leads to nonsense-mediated decay or a non-functional, shortened polypeptide.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A neonate presents with features of Down Syndrome, but the karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, including a fusion of the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21. Name and describe this mutation.
back:
• Robertsonian Translocation
• Fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes at their centromeres.
• Loss of short (p) arms occurs, while long (q) arms form a single large chromosome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural DNA alteration found in a chromosomal inversion and its effect on the genetic sequence.
back:
• A chromosome segment breaks, flips 180 degrees, and reinserts.
• The linear order of genes is reversed.
• Usually balanced (no gain/loss of material) but can disrupt genes at breakpoints.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The presence of two or more cell lines with different genotypes in a single individual, arising from post-zygotic mitotic errors, is termed [___].
back:
• Mosaicism
• Caused by nondisjunction during mitosis in early embryonic development.
• Results in a mixture of normal and abnormal cells (e.g., Mosaic Down Syndrome).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A clinical report mentions a 'microdeletion' on chromosome 22q11.2. Explain the likely effect of this mutation on gene dosage.
back:
• Results in partial monosomy for the affected region.
• Causes haploinsufficiency, where a single functional copy is insufficient.
• Often leads to complex multi-system syndromes (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Differentiate between a paracentric and a pericentric inversion based on the involvement of the centromere.
back:
• Paracentric: Inversion occurs within one arm; does not include the centromere.
• Pericentric: Inversion involves both arms; includes the centromere.
• Pericentric inversions may change the relative lengths of the chromosome arms.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the genomic effects of an insertion mutation with those of a translocation.
back:
• Insertion: A DNA segment is added into a chromosome (internal change).
• Translocation: A segment is transferred from one chromosome to a non-homologous chromosome.
• Translocations involve inter-chromosomal exchange; insertions are typically intra-chromosomal additions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Define a 'Silent Mutation' in the context of the degeneracy of the genetic code.
back:
• A point mutation that changes a codon but results in the same amino acid.
• Possible because multiple codons can encode a single amino acid.
• Typically occurs at the third position (wobble) of the codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that replaces a sense codon with a stop codon, causing premature termination of the polypeptide chain, is termed a [___] mutation.
back: - Nonsense mutation. - Leads to a truncated and usually non-functional protein. - May trigger the eukaryotic nonsense-mediated mRNA decay pathway. - Significantly alters the primary structure of the gene product.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent pulmonary infections and malabsorption. Genetic analysis reveals a deletion of three nucleotides (CTT) at the 508th position of the CFTR gene. Identify the mutation classification.
back: - In-frame deletion. - Results in the loss of a single amino acid (Phenylalanine). - Does not shift the triplet reading frame. - Impairs protein folding and leads to proteasomal degradation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the molecular mechanism by which a frameshift mutation alters the translation of a genetic sequence.
back: - Involves the insertion or deletion of nucleotides not divisible by three. - Shifts the entire reading frame of the mRNA. - Alters every amino acid downstream from the mutation site. - Usually creates a premature stop codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast paracentric and pericentric chromosomal inversions based on the involvement of the centromere and the resulting morphology.
back: - Paracentric: Involves a single arm; does not include the centromere. - Pericentric: Involves both arms; includes the centromere. - Pericentric inversions may change the length ratio of the short and long arms.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the structural rearrangement that occurs during a Robertsonian Translocation involving human acrocentric chromosomes.
back: - Fusion of the long (q) arms of two acrocentric chromosomes. - Occurs at the centromeres. - Results in the loss of the short (p) arms. - The individual typically has 45 chromosomes but remains phenotypically normal.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: When an individual possesses two or more genetically distinct cell populations originating from a single zygote, the condition is known as [___].
back: - Mosaicism. - Often caused by mitotic non-disjunction during early embryonic development. - Clinical severity depends on the timing of the mutation and the specific tissues involved. - Common in some cases of Down syndrome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient presents with symptoms of anemia and vaso-occlusive crises. Sequencing reveals a GAG to GTG mutation at codon 6 of the beta-globin gene. Identify the mutation type.
back: - Missense point mutation. - A single base substitution changes one amino acid to another (Glutamate to Valine). - Changes the biochemical properties of the hemoglobin molecule. - Leads to polymerization of hemoglobin under deoxygenated conditions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain how an in-frame insertion of three nucleotides affects the primary structure of a protein compared to a frameshift insertion.
back: - In-frame insertion: Adds specific amino acids without altering the downstream sequence. - Frameshift: Alters all subsequent amino acids due to reading frame displacement. - In-frame mutations are generally less disruptive than frameshift mutations.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the nucleotide substitutions in transition mutations with those found in transversion mutations.
back: - Transition: Replacement of a purine with another purine (A/G) or pyrimidine with a pyrimidine (C/T). - Transversion: Replacement of a purine with a pyrimidine or vice versa. - Transitions are statistically more common during DNA replication.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: State the biological consequence of a silent mutation on the final protein product.
back: - No change in the amino acid sequence. - Result of genetic code degeneracy/redundancy. - Often occurs at the third nucleotide of a codon. - The protein's primary, secondary, and tertiary structures remain completely normal.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A mutation where a single nucleotide base is replaced by another, potentially resulting in a silent, missense, or nonsense effect, is known as a [___].
back:
• Point mutation
• Can be transitions (purine to purine) or transversions (purine to pyrimidine)
• May result in a single amino acid change or premature termination.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient’s genetic report shows a mutation in the β-globin gene where GAG is replaced by GTG, leading to valine instead of glutamate. Identify the specific point mutation type.
back:
• Missense Mutation
• Results in a different amino acid being incorporated
• Underlying cause of Sickle Cell Anemia
• Alters protein structure and function.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the impact of an insertion of two nucleotides into the coding region of a gene on the resulting protein product.
back:
• Frameshift mutation
• Shifts the triplet reading frame downstream
• Leads to an entirely different amino acid sequence
• Frequently creates a premature stop codon/truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A newborn presents with features of Down Syndrome, but the karyotype shows 46 chromosomes with a fusion of 14q and 21q. Contrast this with standard Trisomy 21.
back:
• Robertsonian Translocation
• Fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes at centromeres
• Involves loss of short arms (p-arms)
• Standard Trisomy 21 involves 47 chromosomes via non-disjunction.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: How does a nonsense mutation specifically alter the translation process of a polypeptide?
back:
• Changes a sense codon to a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA)
• Causes premature termination of translation
• Produces a truncated, usually non-functional protein
• Often leads to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The condition where an individual possesses two or more genetically different cell lines derived from a single zygote is called [___].
back:
• Mosaicism
• Occurs due to post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction
• Severity of symptoms depends on the proportion of affected cells
• Common in Turner or Down Syndrome variants.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Genetic analysis of a patient with Cystic Fibrosis reveals a deletion of three nucleotides (CTT) at the 508th position. Describe the effect on the reading frame.
back:
• In-frame deletion (ΔF508)
• Reading frame remains unchanged
• Single amino acid (Phenylalanine) is lost
• Leads to protein misfolding and proteasomal degradation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural consequence of a chromosomal inversion and its effect on genetic material quantity.
back:
• Chromosome segment is reversed 180 degrees
• Paracentric (excludes centromere) or Pericentric (includes centromere)
• Balanced rearrangement; no net loss/gain of genetic material
• May cause infertility/unbalanced gametes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the genetic outcome of a Large Deletion versus an Insertion on a chromosome segment.
back:
• Deletion: Loss of DNA; leads to haploinsufficiency (e.g., Cri-du-chat)
• Insertion: Addition of DNA; can disrupt gene sequences or cause frameshifts
• Both can result in unbalanced karyotypes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the purine-to-purine point mutation where Adenine is replaced by Guanine.
back:
• Transition mutation
• Substitution within the same chemical class
• Contrast with Transversion (purine to pyrimidine)
• More common than transversions in the human genome.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that results in the premature termination of a polypeptide chain due to the creation of a stop codon is classified as a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation
• Converts a sense codon (e.g., UCA) into a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA)
• Results in a truncated, usually nonfunctional protein product

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient presents with painful crises and anemia. Genetic testing reveals a single nucleotide substitution (A to T) in the β-globin gene, replacing Glutamate with Valine. Identify this mutation type.
back:
• Missense mutation
• A point mutation where a single base change results in a different amino acid
• Can alter the protein's native folding and biological activity

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the molecular mechanism and downstream effect of a frameshift mutation on the resulting protein product.
back:
• Caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of three
• Shifts the reading frame from the point of mutation
• Leads to a radically different amino acid sequence
• Often creates a premature stop codon

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the effect on the reading frame of a 1-base deletion versus a 3-base in-frame deletion (such as the ΔF508 mutation in Cystic Fibrosis).
back:
• 1-base deletion: Disrupts the reading frame (frameshift), altering all subsequent amino acids
• 3-base deletion: Maintains the reading frame (in-frame)
• Result of 3-base: Loss of a single amino acid residue, typically causing misfolding

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural outcome of a Robertsonian Translocation involving acrocentric chromosomes.
back:
• Fusion of the long arms (q-arms) of two acrocentric chromosomes
• Short arms (p-arms) are typically lost
• Reduces total chromosome count to 45
• Often involves chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A chromosomal rearrangement where a segment of DNA is flipped 180 degrees within the same chromosome is known as an [___].
back:
• Inversion
• Pericentric involves the centromere; Paracentric does not
• Usually a balanced rearrangement with no loss of genetic material
• May disrupt genes at the breakpoints

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A child is diagnosed with Down Syndrome but exhibits milder features. Karyotyping reveals some cells with 46 chromosomes and others with 47 (Trisomy 21). Identify the genetic phenomenon.
back:
• Mosaicism
• Presence of two or more genetically distinct cell lines in one individual
• Usually results from post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction
• Phenotype severity depends on the proportion of abnormal cells

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism by which trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene coding region causes disease.
back:
• Expansion of tandem CAG repeats results in extra Glutamine residues
• Produces a toxic 'gain-of-function' protein
• The abnormally long protein fragments aggregate within neurons
• Leads to progressive neurodegeneration

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between silent and missense point mutations regarding their effect on the final protein structure.
back:
• Silent: Base change codes for the same amino acid; no change in protein sequence
• Missense: Base change codes for a different amino acid; alters primary structure
• Silent mutations occur due to the degeneracy of the genetic code

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Define a chromosomal insertion and identify its most common impact on protein-coding sequences.
back:
• Addition of one or more nucleotides into a DNA segment
• If not in multiples of three, it causes a frameshift mutation
• Frequently results in loss of protein function due to altered sequences

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that results in the premature appearance of a termination codon (UAG, UAA, or UGA) is specifically termed a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation
• Truncates the polypeptide chain
• Results in a shortened, usually nonfunctional protein
• Can trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A child is diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. Genetic analysis reveals a deletion of one nucleotide in an exon of the dystrophin gene. Describe the effect on the protein product.
back:
• Frameshift mutation occurs
• Alters the entire downstream reading frame
• Results in a completely different amino acid sequence
• Frequently creates a premature stop codon

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the structural mechanism involved in a Robertsonian Translocation between two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21).
back:
• Breaks occur at the centromeres
• Long arms (q) fuse into a single large chromosome
• Short arms (p) are lost
• Reduces total chromosome count to 45

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the genomic consequences of a large chromosomal deletion with those of a paracentric inversion.
back:
• Deletion: Results in loss of genetic material and potential haploinsufficiency
• Inversion: Reverses segment orientation without material loss (balanced)
• Inversion may disrupt genes at breakpoints or affect regulation

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Discuss the developmental origin of mosaicism in an individual displaying a 45,X/46,XX karyotype.
back:
• Caused by post-zygotic mitotic error
• Occurs during early embryonic cleavage
• Results in two or more genetically distinct cell lines
• Degree of phenotype depends on percentage of affected cells

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: In Sickle Cell Anemia, a single nucleotide substitution (GAG to GTG) causing glutamate to be replaced by valine is a classic example of a [___] mutation.
back:
• Missense mutation
• Changes a single amino acid in the polypeptide
• Can be conservative (similar properties) or non-conservative
• Directly alters protein folding and biological function

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 40-year-old male presents with chorea and dementia. Imaging shows caudate atrophy, and genetics reveal an expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene. Identify this type of mutation.
back:
• Trinucleotide repeat expansion (Insertion)
• Results in an abnormally long polyglutamine tract
• Leads to toxic gain-of-function and protein aggregation
• Demonstrates anticipation in subsequent generations

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Detail the mechanical difference in the reading frame between a 3-base pair deletion (like ΔF508 in Cystic Fibrosis) and a 1-base pair deletion.
back:
• 3-bp deletion: In-frame; loses one amino acid but maintains downstream sequence
• 1-bp deletion: Frameshift; shifts the entire triplet reading frame
• 1-bp mutations are usually more severe due to global sequence alteration

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between pericentric and paracentric inversions based on their relationship to the centromere.
back:
• Pericentric: Inversion involves the centromere and both chromosome arms
• Paracentric: Inversion occurs within one arm; does not involve the centromere
• Both are balanced rearrangements that preserve total genetic material

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the type of point mutation that occurs when a nucleotide change results in the same amino acid due to genetic code redundancy.
back:
• Silent mutation
• Amino acid sequence remains unchanged
• Usually involves the third base of a codon (Wobble position)
• Typically has no effect on phenotype

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
