front: A point mutation that results in the premature termination of a polypeptide chain by creating a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) is specifically termed a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation
• Results in a truncated, usually non-functional protein
• Can lead to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A child is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. Genetic testing reveals a three-nucleotide deletion (ΔF508). Explain why this specific mutation does not cause a frameshift.
back:
• It is an in-frame deletion
• Deletion of three bases (one full codon) maintains the downstream triplet reading frame
• Leads to loss of phenylalanine without altering subsequent amino acids

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the structural mechanism behind a Robertsonian Translocation and its effect on the chromosome count.
back:
• Occurs between two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 13, 14, 15, 21, 22)
• Long arms (q) fuse at the centromere; short arms (p) are lost
• Reduces total chromosome count to 45 in carriers

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient presents with phenotypic features of Down Syndrome, but a karyotype shows some cells with 47,XY,+21 and others with 46,XY. Describe the likely underlying mechanism.
back:
• Mosaicism
• Caused by mitotic non-disjunction after fertilization (post-zygotic)
• Results in two or more genetically different cell lines in one individual

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the genetic outcome of an 'Inversion' with that of a 'Deletion' regarding total genetic material.
back:
• Inversion: Balanced rearrangement; no loss or gain of genetic material (segment rotates 180°)
• Deletion: Unbalanced mutation; involves loss of DNA segments
• Inversions often have no phenotype unless a gene is disrupted

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The genetic code's redundancy often allows a single base change at the third position of a codon to have no effect on the amino acid sequence, a phenomenon known as a [___] mutation.
back:
• Silent mutation
• Often occurs at the 'wobble' position
• Nucleotide change results in a synonymous codon

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: In Sickle Cell Anemia, a point mutation in the β-globin gene replaces Glutamate with Valine. Identify the classification of this mutation based on the protein product.
back:
• Missense mutation
• Substitution of one amino acid for another
• Changes protein chemistry (hydrophilic to hydrophobic), causing polymerization of HbS

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe how the insertion of a single nucleotide into an exon typically results in a non-functional protein product.
back:
• Causes a frameshift mutation
• Shifts the entire triplet reading frame downstream
• Usually introduces a premature stop codon, leading to truncation

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between Paracentric and Pericentric chromosomal inversions.
back:
• Paracentric: Does not involve the centromere
• Pericentric: Involves the centromere and involves both arms
• Pericentric inversions can change the p:q arm ratio

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Identify the type of point mutation that occurs when a Purine is replaced by a Pyrimidine.
back:
• Transversion
• Example: Adenine (Purine) replaced by Cytosine (Pyrimidine)
• Contrast with Transition (Purine to Purine or Pyrimidine to Pyrimidine)

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A point mutation that results in the premature termination of a polypeptide chain by converting a sense codon into a stop codon is known as a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation.
• Creates stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA).
• Results in a truncated, usually non-functional protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy has a deletion of two nucleotides in the dystrophin gene. This leads to a [___].
back:
• Frameshift mutation.
• Alters the reading frame downstream from the mutation.
• Usually creates a premature stop codon.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural mechanism that differentiates a Robertsonian Translocation from a standard reciprocal translocation.
back:
• Occurs only between acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22).
• Fusion of long arms (q) at the centromere.
• Short arms (p) are lost.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between pericentric and paracentric chromosomal inversions regarding their involvement with the centromere.
back:
• Pericentric: Includes the centromere; can change the arm-length ratio.
• Paracentric: Involves only one arm; does not include the centromere.
• Both involve 180-degree segment rotation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the biological cause of mosaicism in an individual presenting with both 45,X and 46,XX cell lines.
back:
• Mitotic nondisjunction.
• Occurs post-fertilization (post-zygotic).
• Results in genetically distinct cell populations in one individual.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A mutation that swaps a single nucleotide but does not change the resulting amino acid due to the degeneracy of the genetic code is a [___] mutation.
back:
• Silent mutation.
• Often involves the third base (wobble position).
• Phenotype remains normal.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: In Sickle Cell Anemia, a GAG to GTG substitution at codon 6 of the β-globin gene replaces glutamate with valine. Identify the type of mutation.
back:
• Missense mutation.
• Point mutation changing one amino acid.
• Results in altered protein structure/function.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain how trinucleotide repeat expansions (e.g., CAG in Huntington disease) disrupt a DNA segment.
back:
• Specialized insertion mutation.
• Number of tandem repeats increases beyond the stable threshold.
• Causes toxic protein gain-of-function or gene silencing.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the impact on the reading frame between a 3-base deletion and a 1-base deletion in an exon.
back:
• 3-base: In-frame; deletes one amino acid but preserves the rest of the sequence.
• 1-base: Frameshift; disrupts all subsequent amino acids.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Name the condition where a lost chromosomal segment results in Cri-du-chat syndrome.
back:
• Chromosomal Deletion.
• Specifically terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-).
• Results in haploinsufficiency of genes in that region.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The directional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and subsequently to protein is a principle referred to as the [___].
back:
• Central Dogma.
• Involves replication, transcription, and translation.
• Describes the conversion of genotype to phenotype.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A neonate with microcytic anemia is found to have a mutation creating a new splice site in the β-globin gene. This defect interferes with which phase of the central dogma?
back:
• Post-transcriptional processing.
• Specifically affects splicing of pre-mRNA.
• Leads to abnormal mRNA and defective protein synthesis.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the mechanism by which tRNA molecules ensure the correct amino acid is incorporated into a polypeptide chain during translation.
back:
• Anticodon on tRNA pairs with mRNA codon.
• Follows complementary and antiparallel base-pairing rules.
• Wobble hypothesis allows flexible pairing at the third codon position.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the spatial and temporal relationship of transcription and translation in prokaryotes versus eukaryotes.
back:
• Prokaryotes: Simultaneous/coupled (no nuclear membrane).
• Eukaryotes: Separated; transcription occurs in nucleus, translation in cytoplasm.
• Eukaryotic mRNA requires export before translation.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Detail the energetic cost (high-energy bonds) required for the addition of one amino acid to a growing polypeptide chain.
back:
• 4 total high-energy bonds.
• 2 from ATP (tRNA charging/aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase).
• 1 from GTP (tRNA binding to A-site).
• 1 from GTP (translocation).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: In eukaryotic mRNA, the consensus sequence AAUAAA found near the 3' end is essential for the process of [___].
back:
• Polyadenylation (Poly-A tailing).
• Signal for endonuclease cleavage and tail addition.
• Enhances mRNA stability and nuclear export.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient is treated for tuberculosis with Rifampin. Explain the biochemical target of this drug regarding the central dogma.
back:
• Targets Prokaryotic RNA Polymerase (beta subunit).
• Specifically inhibits the initiation of transcription.
• Prevents synthesis of the primary mRNA transcript.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain how the degeneracy of the genetic code protects an organism against certain types of point mutations.
back:
• Silent mutations: Multiple codons specify the same amino acid.
• Mutation in the third base often results in no change to the protein.
• Minimizes deleterious effects of DNA replication errors.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between the roles of the P-site and A-site on the ribosome during the elongation phase of translation.
back:
• A-site (Aminoacyl): Binds the incoming charged tRNA.
• P-site (Peptidyl): Holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide chain.
• Peptidyl transferase catalyzes the bond between them.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: State the function of the TATA (Hogness) box in the initiation of eukaryotic transcription.
back:
• Core promoter element located ~25 bases upstream.
• Binding site for Transcription Factor IID (TFIID).
• Directs RNA Polymerase II to the correct start site.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A mutation where a single nucleotide change results in a codon that still codes for the same amino acid due to genetic code degeneracy is known as a [___] mutation.
back:
Silent Mutation:
* Usually involves the third base (wobble position) of a codon.
* No change occurs in the primary amino acid sequence of the protein.
* Maintains normal protein function and phenotype.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A 4-month-old child presents with severe anemia. Genetic sequencing reveals a single nucleotide insertion in the coding region of the β-globin gene, resulting in a completely altered amino acid sequence downstream. Identify this mutation type.
back:
Frameshift Mutation:
* Occurs when insertions/deletions are not multiples of three.
* Shifts the mRNA reading frame during translation.
* Often creates a premature stop codon, leading to truncated or non-functional proteins.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the molecular mechanism and outcome of a nonsense mutation on a segment of DNA during translation.
back:
Premature Termination:
* A point mutation changes a sense codon into a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA).
* Translation terminates early, producing a truncated polypeptide.
* Frequently leads to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, reducing total protein levels.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the structural involvement of the centromere in pericentric versus paracentric chromosomal inversions.
back:
Centromere Involvement:
* Pericentric: The inversion includes the centromere; breaks occur in both the p and q arms.
* Paracentric: The centromere is excluded; breaks occur within a single arm.
* Both involve 180-degree rotation of DNA segments.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural reconfiguration involved in a Robertsonian Translocation between acrocentric chromosomes.
back:
Acrocentric Fusion:
* Long arms (q) of two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) fuse at the centromere.
* The short arms (p) are typically lost.
* Results in 45 chromosomes in balanced carriers; often leads to trisomies in offspring.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The presence of two or more cell lines with different genotypes in a single individual, arising from post-fertilization mitotic nondisjunction, is termed [___].
back:
Mosaicism:
* Originates from a single zygote through error during early mitosis.
* Clinical severity is dictated by the percentage and distribution of abnormal cells.
* Commonly observed in mosaic Down Syndrome (46/47 chromosomes).

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient is diagnosed with Sickle Cell Anemia. The molecular defect involves a point mutation changing GAG to GTG, replacing Glutamate with Valine. Classify this mutation based on its effect on the protein.
back:
Missense Mutation:
* A single base substitution results in a different amino acid.
* Changes the biochemical property of the protein (hydrophilic to hydrophobic).
* Leads to polymerization of HbS under deoxygenated conditions.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Discuss the mechanism by which trinucleotide repeat expansions affect DNA segments and lead to neurodegenerative disorders like Huntington’s disease.
back:
Tandem Amplification:
* Specific triplets (e.g., CAG) increase in number during DNA replication.
* Expansion beyond a threshold causes protein aggregation or gene silencing.
* Exhibit 'anticipation,' where severity increases in successive generations.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Distinguish between the structural effects of a chromosomal deletion versus a chromosomal insertion on a segment of DNA.
back:
DNA Content Change:
* Deletion: Loss of one or more nucleotides; may involve whole genes or small segments.
* Insertion: Gain of exogenous nucleotides within a DNA sequence.
* Both cause frameshifts if the count is not a multiple of three.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Define a 'transversion' in the context of point mutations and distinguish it from a 'transition'.
back:
Nucleotide Substitution:
* Transversion: A purine (A, G) is replaced by a pyrimidine (C, T) or vice versa.
* Transition: Replacement of a purine with another purine, or pyrimidine with another pyrimidine.
* Transitions are generally more common in the genome.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and finally to protein is known as the [___].
back: • Central Dogma • Describes the sequential transfer of information • DNA acts as the repository • RNA acts as the intermediate messenger

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A researcher identifies a virus that uses its RNA genome to synthesize DNA within a host cell. This process diverges from the traditional central dogma via the enzyme [___].
back: • Reverse Transcriptase • Synthesizes DNA from an RNA template • Characteristic of retroviruses like HIV • Essential for integrating viral genes into the host genome

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the biological role of RNA Polymerase II in the execution of the central dogma.
back: • Synthesizes mRNA precursors (hnRNA) • Transcribes the majority of protein-coding genes • Recognizes core promoter elements like the TATA box • Subject to regulation by transcription factors

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient is diagnosed with a genetic disorder caused by a base substitution. Contrast the effect on the central dogma if this results in a nonsense mutation versus a frameshift mutation.
back: • Nonsense: Creates a premature stop codon, leading to truncated proteins • Frameshift: Deletion/insertion alters the reading frame, changing all subsequent amino acids and often causing distal stops

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain how the 'Degeneracy' of the genetic code maintains the fidelity of protein synthesis despite point mutations.
back: • Multiple codons specify the same amino acid • Mutations at the third base (wobble position) often result in silent mutations • Minimizes the phenotypic impact of genetic errors

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The process of synthesizing a specific polypeptide chain from an mRNA template on the ribosome is termed [___].
back: • Translation • Converts nucleotide 'language' to amino acid 'language' • Requires tRNA, rRNA, and mRNA • Driven by ATP and GTP hydrolysis

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A child presents with severe anemia due to Beta-Thalassemia. Testing reveals a mutation in a consensus sequence at an intron-exon junction. Identify the defective post-transcriptional process.
back: • RNA Splicing • Mediated by the spliceosome (snRNPs) • Removal of non-coding introns and joining of exons • Failure leads to aberrant mRNA and non-functional proteins

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: How do eukaryotic cells prevent the translation of raw, unprocessed genomic transcripts in the cytoplasm?
back: • Spatial separation: Transcription occurs in the nucleus • Nuclear export requires 5' capping and 3' polyadenylation • Initiation factors (eIFs) specifically recognize the 7-methylguanosine cap for ribosome assembly

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between the Template Strand and the Coding Strand during the transcription phase of the central dogma.
back: • Template: The antisense strand read 3' to 5' by RNA polymerase • Coding: The sense strand with a sequence identical to the synthesized RNA (U replaces T)

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the three-nucleotide sequence on mRNA that establishes the reading frame and initiates the central dogma's final step.
back: • AUG (Start Codon) • Specifies the amino acid Methionine (formylated in prokaryotes) • Positions the small ribosomal subunit correctly on the mRNA

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A [___] mutation involves the substitution of a single nucleotide base for another without altering the total length of the DNA segment.
back: * Substitution of one base pair. * Classified as silent, missense, or nonsense. * Does not shift the reading frame.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A young child presents with thick respiratory secretions and pancreatic insufficiency. Genetic analysis reveals a three-nucleotide deletion at codon 508. Identify the mutation type and its effect on the reading frame.
back: * In-frame deletion. * Reading frame remains intact. * Specific amino acid (phenylalanine) is lost. * Leads to protein misfolding and degradation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism by which a frameshift mutation, caused by a DNA insertion, carries out its biological impact during the translation of a protein.
back: * Shifts the triplet reading frame. * Incorrect amino acids incorporated downstream. * Often creates a premature stop codon. * Results in a non-functional, truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A mother is found to have a balanced reciprocal translocation. Contrast her clinical phenotype with the risk to her potential offspring.
back: * Mother: Usually phenotypically normal (balanced dosage). * Offspring: Risk of unbalanced gametes. * May result in partial trisomy or monosomy. * Increased risk of miscarriage or congenital anomalies.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the structural change to a DNA segment during a chromosomal inversion mutation.
back: * DNA segment breaks at two points. * Segment rotates 180 degrees. * Reinserted into the same locus. * Pericentric involves centromere; paracentric does not.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: The addition of one or more extra nucleotides into a segment of DNA is known as an [___].
back: * Insertion. * Increases nucleotide count. * Can cause a frameshift if not in multiples of three. * Disrupts the existing gene sequence.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient with Down Syndrome features has two genetically distinct cell lines: one with 47,XY,+21 and one with 46,XY. Name this condition and its developmental timing.
back: * Chromosomal Mosaicism. * Occurs post-fertilization (post-zygotic). * Result of mitotic nondisjunction. * Phenotype depends on the ratio of normal cells.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Explain the mechanism of a Robertsonian Translocation and its effect on the short (p) arms of the chromosomes involved.
back: * Fusion of long arms (q) of acrocentric chromosomes. * Occurs at centromeres. * Short (p) arms are lost (repetitive rRNA genes). * Balanced carriers have 45 chromosomes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast a DNA deletion mutation with a DNA insertion mutation regarding their effect on the length of a chromosome segment.
back: * Deletion: Nucleotides are removed, decreasing segment length. * Insertion: Nucleotides are added, increasing segment length. * Both can cause frameshifts if not in multiples of three.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the specific effect of a nonsense point mutation on the resulting polypeptide chain.
back: * Substitution creates a premature stop codon. * (UAA, UAG, or UGA). * Translation terminates early. * Produces a truncated, usually non-functional protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A [___] mutation occurs when a single nucleotide base is changed, potentially resulting in a silent, missense, or nonsense effect.
back: * Point Mutation. * Silent: Changes the DNA sequence without altering the amino acid. * Missense: Results in a different amino acid being inserted. * Nonsense: Creates a premature stop codon, terminating translation.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: A patient's genetic report indicates a 1-base pair deletion within an exon. Describe the likely impact on the resulting protein's primary structure.
back: * Frameshift mutation. * Alters the downstream reading frame from the point of mutation. * Results in a radically different amino acid sequence. * Often leads to a premature stop codon and truncated protein.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Describe the role of acrocentric chromosomes in the formation of a Robertsonian Translocation.
back: * Involves acrocentric chromosomes like 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22. * Fusion occurs at the centromeres. * Short arms are lost while long arms join into a single hybrid chromosome. * Balanced carriers have forty-five chromosomes.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the molecular result of a 3-base pair deletion (like ΔF508 in CF) with a 1-base pair deletion regarding the protein's reading frame.
back: * 3-base deletion: No frameshift occurs because the triplet reading frame is maintained; one amino acid is lost. * 1-base deletion: Causes a frameshift mutation. * Impact: Frameshifts radically alter all downstream amino acids and protein function.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Analyze how gene amplification of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) contributes to cellular resistance against methotrexate therapy.
back: * Increased gene copy number leads to overproduction of the target enzyme. * Excess DHFR allows continued thymidine triphosphate synthesis despite drug presence. * The drug's competitive inhibition is overcome by the high intracellular enzyme concentration.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: In the context of Down Syndrome, the presence of two distinct cell lines due to post-zygotic mitotic nondisjunction is referred to as [___].
back: * Mosaicism. * Defined as the presence of genetically distinct cell lines in one individual. * Often results in a milder clinical presentation. * Diagnosed by identifying a mixture of normal and abnormal cells in the karyotype.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Molecular analysis reveals a GAG to GTG transversion in the β-globin gene. Identify the specific type of point mutation and its effect on the hemoglobin protein.
back: * Missense Mutation. * Results in the substitution of Valine for Glutamic Acid at position 6. * Creates abnormal Hemoglobin S (HbS). * Promotes deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerization and subsequent red cell sickling.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Detail the mechanism by which a reciprocal translocation can lead to partial trisomy or monosomy in offspring.
back: * Segments are exchanged between non-homologous chromosomes. * Balanced carriers have the correct amount of material but produce unbalanced gametes. * Zygotes inherit extra or missing DNA segments, leading to severe developmental defects or miscarriage.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Contrast the effects of iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) on the translation of ferritin mRNA versus transferrin receptor mRNA when cellular iron is low.
back: * Ferritin: IRP binds the 5-prime iron responsive element, blocking translation. * Transferrin Receptor: IRP binds the 3-prime iron responsive element, stabilizing the mRNA. * Result: Net effect increases iron uptake while decreasing iron storage.

category: Describe the effect of the following chromosomal mutations on a segment of DNA: point mutation, frameshift mutation, deletion, insertion, inversion, Robertsonian Translocation and mosaicism
front: Specify the primary difference between a deletion and an insertion mutation regarding the DNA segment length.
back: * Deletion: One or more nucleotides are removed, shortening the DNA segment. * Insertion: One or more nucleotides are added, lengthening the DNA segment. * Both cause frameshifts if the count is not a multiple of three.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The biological principle describing the unidirectional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and finally to protein is known as the [___].
back: • Central Dogma • Involves replication, transcription, and translation. • Exceptions include reverse transcription in retroviruses.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient is infected with a retrovirus that violates the standard central dogma by using an enzyme to synthesize DNA from an RNA template. This enzyme is [___].
back: • Reverse Transcriptase • RNA-dependent DNA polymerase. • Crucial for viral integration into the host genome.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain the role of the 7-methylguanosine cap and the poly-A tail in the maturation of eukaryotic mRNA transcripts.
back: • 5' Cap: Facilitates translation initiation and protects against nucleases. • 3' Tail: Aids nuclear export and stabilizes the transcript. • Both are absent in prokaryotic mRNA.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A researcher identifies a mutation in a gene. Contrast the cellular outcome if this results in a missense mutation versus a nonsense mutation.
back: • Missense: One amino acid is replaced by another; may alter protein function. • Nonsense: Creates a premature stop codon; results in a truncated, often non-functional protein.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Summarize the primary mechanism by which aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases ensure the accuracy of the translation process.
back: • Matches specific amino acids to their corresponding tRNAs. • Uses ATP to activate the amino acid. • Possesses editing/proofreading activity to remove incorrect amino acids.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: During the processing of hnRNA in eukaryotes, non-coding intervening sequences called [___] are removed to produce mature mRNA.
back: • Introns • Removed by the spliceosome (snRNPs). • Exons are joined together to form the coding sequence.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: In a child diagnosed with a type of β-thalassemia, a mutation affects a splice site. Describe the likely impact on the hemoglobin protein produced.
back: • Incorrect intron removal or exon skipping. • Inclusion of non-coding sequences leads to a frameshift or early termination. • Results in a deficiency of functional β-globin chains.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the mechanism of the Shine-Dalgarno sequence in prokaryotes and contrast its function with the eukaryotic 'scanning' model.
back: • Prokaryotes: 16S rRNA binds the Shine-Dalgarno sequence to align the AUG start codon. • Eukaryotes: Small ribosomal subunit binds the 5' cap and scans for the first AUG. • Prokaryotes can be polycistronic due to this sequence.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the 'degeneracy' and 'specificity' characteristics of the genetic code.
back: • Degeneracy: Multiple codons can code for one amino acid (e.g., Leucine). • Specificity: One specific codon always codes for the same amino acid (unambiguous).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the three major types of RNA involved in translation and their primary roles.
back: • mRNA: Carries the genetic message from DNA. • tRNA: Acts as an adaptor carrying specific amino acids. • rRNA: Structural/catalytic component of the ribosome.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The unidirectional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and then to protein is known as the [___].
back:
• Central Dogma of molecular biology
• Describes the sequential transfer of information
• Key steps: Transcription (DNA to RNA) and Translation (RNA to protein)

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient with tuberculosis is treated with Rifampin. Describe the specific molecular target and process inhibited by this drug.
back:
• Target: Beta-subunit of bacterial RNA Polymerase
• Process: Transcription initiation
• Effect: Prevents synthesis of mRNA from the DNA template

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain how the prokaryotic 30S ribosomal subunit correctly identifies the mRNA start site for translation.
back:
• 16S rRNA base-pairs with the Shine-Dalgarno sequence
• Positions the ribosome near the AUG start codon
• Ensures translation begins in the correct reading frame

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the molecular purpose of eukaryotic RNA splicing with post-translational proteolytic trimming.
back:
• Splicing: Removes non-coding introns to join exons in pre-mRNA
• Trimming: Cleaves peptide bonds to activate pro-proteins (e.g., insulin)
• Timing: Splicing is pre-translational; trimming is post-translational

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the enzymatic exception to the classic DNA-to-RNA flow utilized by retroviruses.
back:
• Enzyme: Reverse Transcriptase
• Mechanism: RNA-directed DNA polymerase
• Function: Synthesizes DNA using a viral RNA template for integration

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The property of the genetic code where a single amino acid is specified by multiple different codons is defined as [___].
back:
• Degeneracy (or redundancy)
• Significance: Minimizes the phenotypic impact of point mutations
• Mechanism: Often involves 'wobble' pairing at the third codon base

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
coreConcept: Molecular Basis of Sickle Cell Anemia
front: In Sickle Cell Anemia, a point mutation (GAG to GTG) results in valine replacing glutamate. Classify this mutation type and its direct effect on the central dogma.
back:
• Mutation: Missense mutation
• Effect: Alters the mRNA codon during transcription
• Result: Changes the primary amino acid sequence during translation

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: How does aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase ensure the fidelity of the central dogma before the ribosome is involved?
back:
• Specificity: Correctly matches amino acids to their cognate tRNAs
• Activation: Utilizes ATP to form a high-energy ester bond
• Proofreading: Contains an editing site to hydrolyze incorrect pairings

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between polycistronic and monocistronic mRNA in the context of information flow.
back:
• Polycistronic: One mRNA encodes multiple proteins; characteristic of prokaryotic operons
• Monocistronic: One mRNA encodes one protein; characteristic of eukaryotes
• Eukaryotes require individual promoters for each gene

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the functional role of the Hogness (TATA) box in eukaryotic gene expression.
back:
• Location: Core promoter sequence ~25 bases upstream of start site
• Binding: Recognized by TFIID (General Transcription Factor)
• Function: Directs RNA Polymerase II to the correct start point

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: In the flow of genetic information, the enzyme responsible for synthesizing a primary RNA transcript from a DNA template is [___].
back:
**RNA Polymerase**
* Synthesizes RNA in the 5' to 3' direction.
* Uses ribonucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) as substrates.
* Does not require a primer to initiate synthesis.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A 10-year-old patient with anemia has a GAG to GTG mutation at codon 6 of the beta-globin gene. Identify the mutation type and its specific effect on the protein product.
back:
**Missense Mutation**
* Replaces Glutamate with Valine at position 6.
* Changes the amino acid sequence without altering protein length.
* Results in Hemoglobin S (HbS).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the mechanism by which the primary eukaryotic transcript is converted into mature messenger RNA through the removal of non-coding sequences.
back:
**Splicing**
* Spliceosomes (snRNPs) recognize consensus sequences at intron-exon boundaries.
* Introns are removed as a 'lariat' structure.
* Exons are ligated to form a continuous coding sequence.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the recognition of the translation start site in prokaryotic mRNA versus eukaryotic mRNA systems.
back:
**Initiation Sites**
* Prokaryotes: 16S rRNA binds the **Shine-Dalgarno sequence** upstream of AUG.
* Eukaryotes: The 40S subunit binds the **5' Cap** and scans for the first AUG.
* Eukaryotes utilize many more initiation factors (eIFs).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain the biological significance of the 'Wobble Hypothesis' regarding tRNA-codon recognition.
back:
**Wobble Hypothesis**
* The 5' base of the anticodon is less spatially constrained.
* Allows nontraditional base pairing at the 3' position of the codon.
* Enables one tRNA species to recognize multiple synonymous codons.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The three specific nucleotide triplets that signal the termination of translation are UAA, UAG, and [___].
back:
**UGA**
* Recognized by release factors (RFs) rather than tRNA.
* Triggers the hydrolysis of the bond between the peptide and tRNA.
* Causes the ribosomal complex to dissociate.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Genetic testing for a patient with severe digestive and pulmonary issues reveals a three-base deletion (ΔF508) in the CFTR gene. State the effect of this mutation on the reading frame and protein fate.
back:
**In-frame Deletion**
* Loss of Phenylalanine without shifting the reading frame.
* Leads to abnormal protein folding in the RER.
* Targeted for degradation by the cytosolic proteasome via ubiquitination.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Detail the energetic requirements for adding a single amino acid to a growing polypeptide chain during the elongation phase.
back:
**Energy Consumption**
* 4 high-energy bonds total per amino acid.
* 2 from ATP (tRNA charging/synthetase).
* 1 from GTP (binding aminoacyl-tRNA to A-site).
* 1 from GTP (translocation step).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish the structural modifications found at the 5' and 3' ends of a mature eukaryotic mRNA transcript.
back:
**mRNA Termini**
* 5' End: **7-methylguanosine cap** linked via 5'-to-5' triphosphate bond.
* 3' End: **Poly-A tail** (40-250 adenylates) added by polyadenylate polymerase.
* Both stabilize mRNA and facilitate translation initiation.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the specific three-base sequence located at the 3' end of all transfer RNA molecules where the amino acid is covalently attached.
back:
**CCA Sequence**
* Added post-transcriptionally by nucleotidyltransferase.
* Forms an ester linkage with the amino acid carboxyl group.
* Essential for charging tRNA by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The 'central dogma' of molecular biology describes the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and finally to [___].
back:
● Protein (Polypeptide).
● DNA represents the stored genome.
● RNA serves as the working copy.
● Protein is the functional end-product.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient presents with liver failure after eating wild mushrooms. The toxin α-amanitin in these mushrooms inhibits eukaryotic gene expression by targeting [___].
back:
● RNA Polymerase II.
● It halts messenger RNA (mRNA) synthesis.
● Prevents translation of essential proteins.
● Leads to massive hepatocyte necrosis.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain how the spliceosome distinguishes between coding and non-coding sequences during the processing of eukaryotic pre-mRNA.
back:
● Recognizes invariant GU at the 5' donor site.
● Recognizes invariant AG at the 3' acceptor site.
● Uses snRNPs (U1, U2, etc.) to form a lariat.
● Removes introns and ligates exons.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the mechanism used by the small ribosomal subunit to locate the start codon in prokaryotes versus eukaryotes.
back:
● Prokaryotes: 16S rRNA binds the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
● Eukaryotes: 40S subunit binds the 5' methylguanosine cap.
● Eukaryotes: Ribosome 'scans' until it finds the first AUG.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Name the specific enzyme utilized by exceptions to the traditional central dogma, such as retroviruses or telomerase, to synthesize DNA from RNA.
back:
● Reverse transcriptase.
● Also known as RNA-directed DNA polymerase.
● Synthesizes a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand.
● Essential for HIV replication and telomere maintenance.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: According to the wobble hypothesis, nontraditional base pairing can occur between the first base of the [___] and the third base of the mRNA codon.
back:
● tRNA Anticodon.
● Allows one tRNA to recognize multiple codons.
● Reduces the number of required tRNA species.
● Typically occurs at the 5' end of the anticodon.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A genetic study reveals a mutation changing a Serine codon (UCA) to UAA. Describe the likely effect on the resulting polypeptide chain.
back:
● Nonsense Mutation.
● Creates a premature termination (stop) codon.
● Results in a truncated protein.
● Usually leads to loss of protein function.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the mechanism that targets newly synthesized secretory proteins to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) during translation.
back:
● N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence emerges.
● Signal Recognition Particle (SRP) binds and stalls translation.
● SRP delivers the complex to the RER translocon.
● Translation resumes into the RER lumen.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between monocistronic and polycistronic mRNA in terms of the number of genes encoded per transcript.
back:
● Monocistronic: One mRNA encodes one protein (Eukaryotes).
● Polycistronic: One mRNA encodes multiple proteins (Prokaryotes).
● Prokaryotic genes are often grouped in operons.
● Allows coordinate regulation of metabolic pathways.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the cellular process that converts the language of a nucleotide sequence into the language of an amino acid sequence.
back:
● Translation (Protein Synthesis).
● Occurs on ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
● Requires mRNA, tRNA, and amino acids.
● Uses high-energy bonds from ATP and GTP.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: In prokaryotic replication, the specific protein that recognizes the origin (oriC) and initiates the melting of the DNA helix is [___].
back:
* DnaA protein
* Binds to DnaA boxes within the oriC site
* Facilitates the melting of AT-rich segments
* Requires ATP for activation

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A bacterial culture is treated with a fluoroquinolone antibiotic. Which specific prokaryotic enzyme is targeted to prevent the relief of positive supercoils ahead of the replication fork?
back:
* DNA Gyrase (Type II Topoisomerase)
* Functions to relieve torsional strain
* Introduces negative supercoils using ATP
* Unique target for Ciprofloxacin and Levofloxacin

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Explain how DNA Polymerase III achieves its high processivity during the elongation phase of prokaryotic replication.
back:
* Beta-subunit (sliding clamp) function
* Forms a ring that encircles the DNA
* Prevents the polymerase from dissociating from the template
* Allows continuous synthesis of thousands of nucleotides

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Contrast the 5'→3' exonuclease activity of DNA Polymerase I with the 3'→5' exonuclease activity found in both DNA Polymerase I and III.
back:
* 5'→3' Exonuclease (Pol I only): Excises RNA primers and repairs DNA
* 3'→5' Exonuclease (Both): Provides proofreading by removing mismatched bases
* Pol III lacks 5'→3' exonuclease ability

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Describe the biochemical requirements and role of Primase (DnaG) during lagging strand synthesis.
back:
* Synthesizes short RNA primers (~10 nucleotides)
* Provides the essential 3'-OH group for DNA Pol III
* Repeatedly activated for each Okazaki fragment
* Part of the primosome complex

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: The enzyme responsible for sealing the 'nicks' between Okazaki fragments by creating a phosphodiester bond is [___].
back:
* DNA Ligase
* Catalyzes bonds between 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate groups
* In bacteria, it typically requires NAD+ as a cofactor
* Essential for completing the lagging strand

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A mutant *E. coli* strain fails to remove RNA primers during DNA replication, resulting in DNA-RNA hybrids. This finding suggests a deficiency in which specific enzyme?
back:
* DNA Polymerase I
* Specifically the 5'→3' exonuclease domain
* Pol I is unique in its ability to excise RNA
* Also fills the resulting gap with DNA

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: How do the Tus protein and Ter sequences coordinate the termination of prokaryotic DNA replication?
back:
* Tus protein binds to Ter (termination) sites
* Acts as a 'contra-helicase' to stop DnaB
* Prevents further unwinding of the replication fork
* Results in the dissociation of the replication complex

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Distinguish the orientation of the leading strand synthesis from the lagging strand synthesis relative to the movement of the replication fork.
back:
* Leading: Synthesized 5'→3' towards the fork (continuous)
* Lagging: Synthesized 5'→3' away from the fork (discontinuous)
* Both utilize template reading in the 3'→5' direction

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Identify the role of Single-Stranded DNA-Binding (SSB) proteins once the DNA helix has been unwound by Helicase.
back:
* Maintain separation of parental strands
* Prevent re-annealing (forming dsDNA)
* Protect single-stranded DNA from nuclease degradation
* Bind cooperatively to the DNA backbone

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: In prokaryotic DNA replication, the [___] protein initiates the process by binding to specific boxes within the oriC region, causing the AT-rich segment to melt.
back:
DnaA protein.
- Recognizes and binds DnaA boxes at the origin (oriC).
- Facilitates the initial melting of the DNA unwinding element (DUE).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A patient with a urinary tract infection is prescribed Ciprofloxacin. This drug inhibits prokaryotic DNA replication by targeting [___].
back:
DNA Gyrase (Type II Topoisomerase).
- It introduces negative supercoils.
- Relieves positive supercoiling/torsional strain ahead of the replication fork.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Describe the primary catalytic and proofreading functions of DNA Polymerase III during prokaryotic chain elongation.
back:
- 5' to 3' polymerase activity for new strand synthesis.
- 3' to 5' exonuclease activity for proofreading.
- High processivity ensured by the beta-clamp (sliding clamp).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Contrast the leading and lagging strands of E. coli regarding their continuity and the number of RNA primers required.
back:
Leading: Continuous synthesis; requires only one RNA primer.
Lagging: Discontinuous (Okazaki fragments); requires multiple RNA primers synthesized by Primase (DnaG).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Identify the unique enzymatic activity of DNA Polymerase I that distinguishes it from DNA Polymerase III and its role in primer management.
back:
5' to 3' exonuclease activity.
- Hydrolytically removes RNA primers.
- Fills resulting gaps with DNA using 5' to 3' polymerase activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: The proteins that bind to single-stranded DNA to prevent re-annealing and protect the template from nuclease degradation are known as [___].
back:
Single-stranded DNA-binding (SSB) proteins.
- Maintain strand separation after helicase activity.
- Prevent hairpins and protect ssDNA from enzymatic cleavage.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A laboratory researcher observes that a bacterial culture treated with a specific antibiotic shows an accumulation of positive supercoils, halting replication. The targeted enzyme is likely [___].
back:
DNA Gyrase.
- Essential for removing positive supercoils created by unwinding.
- Essential for the advancement of the replication fork.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Explain how the replication of the circular prokaryotic chromosome is successfully concluded.
back:
- Mediated by Tus protein binding to Ter (termination) sites.
- Tus-Ter complex blocks the movement of the replication fork.
- Results in the release of two daughter molecules.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Distinguish between DNA Helicase and DNA Topoisomerase in terms of their physical action on the DNA double helix.
back:
Helicase: Breaks hydrogen bonds to unzip strands (requires ATP).
Topoisomerase: Cleaves and reseals the phosphodiester backbone to relieve torsional strain.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Specify the direction in which DNA polymerases read the template versus the direction in which they synthesize the daughter strand.
back:
- Reading: 3' to 5' direction.
- Synthesis: 5' to 3' direction.
- All polymerases require a free 3'-OH group to add nucleotides.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: The specific protein in E. coli that recognizes the origin of replication (oriC) and initiates melting of the AT-rich region is [___].
back:
• DnaA protein.
• Binds to specific DnaA boxes.
• Causes initial strand separation at the DNA unwinding element (DUE).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A patient with a urinary tract infection is prescribed Ciprofloxacin. This antibiotic works by inhibiting the prokaryotic enzyme [___], which is responsible for relieving torsional strain during DNA replication.
back:
• DNA Gyrase (Topoisomerase II).
• Relieves positive supercoiling ahead of the replication fork.
• Introduces negative supercoils using ATP hydrolysis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Explain the role of the RNA primer synthesized by DnaG (Primase) during the initiation of DNA synthesis.
back:
• Provides a free 3'-OH group.
• Required because DNA polymerases cannot initiate synthesis de novo.
• Synthesizes short RNA stretches complementary to the DNA template.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A researcher inhibits the 5' to 3' exonuclease activity in a bacterial culture. Contrast how this specific loss affects DNA Replication compared to a loss of 3' to 5' exonuclease activity.
back:
• 5'→3' loss: Prevents RNA primer removal (DNA Pol I function).
• 3'→5' loss: Impairs proofreading, leading to high mutation rates (DNA Pol I/III).
• Only DNA Pol I possesses 5'→3' exonuclease activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: During the elongation phase of prokaryotic replication, describe the mechanism by which DNA Polymerase III ensures high fidelity of the new strand.
back:
• 3'→5' exonuclease activity (proofreading).
• Recognizes and removes mismatched terminal nucleotides.
• Re-synthesizes the correct sequence in the 5'→3' direction.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: In prokaryotes, the short, discontinuous segments of DNA synthesized on the lagging strand are known as [___] fragments.
back:
• Okazaki fragments.
• Synthesized in the 5'→3' direction away from the replication fork.
• Eventually joined by DNA Ligase via phosphodiester bonds.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: A bacterial cell lacks the DnaB protein, and DNA strands fail to separate after initial melting. Identify this protein's function and its required energy source.
back:
• DNA Helicase.
• Unwinds the double helix at the replication fork.
• Requires energy from ATP hydrolysis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Describe the two distinct enzymatic functions of DNA Polymerase I required to complete Okazaki fragment processing.
back:
• 5'→3' Exonuclease: Removes the RNA primer.
• 5'→3' Polymerase: Fills the gap with deoxyribonucleotides.
• 3'→5' Exonuclease: Proofreads the newly filled gap.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Contrast the biological roles of the DnaA protein versus Single-Stranded Binding (SSB) proteins.
back:
• DnaA: Active initiator that melts/opens the origin (oriC).
• SSB: Passive stabilizer that prevents re-annealing of single strands.
• SSB protects single-stranded DNA from nuclease degradation.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in prokaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on: Different proteins required, Primers, DNA polymerase; their different components and functions, Initiation, elongation and termination of replication, Topoisomerases
front: Identify the protein responsible for terminating prokaryotic DNA replication and the specific DNA sites to which it binds.
back:
• Tus protein (Terminus utilization substance).
• Binds to Ter (termination) sites.
• Physically halts the movement of the replication fork.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The directional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and finally to functional protein is known as the [___].
back:
• Central dogma of molecular biology
• Transcription (DNA to RNA)
• Translation (RNA to Protein)
• Exceptions include reverse transcription in RNA viruses

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A point mutation in the beta-globin gene (GAG to GTG) results in valine replacing glutamate. Identify the mutation style and its outcome.
back:
• Missense mutation
• Leads to Sickle Cell Anemia
• Changes a single amino acid in the polypeptide chain
• Alters protein structure and function

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain how the wobble hypothesis accounts for the redundancy of the genetic code in protein synthesis.
back:
• Relaxed base-pairing at the 3rd codon position
• 5' base of tRNA anticodon is less spatially constrained
• Allows one tRNA to recognize multiple synonymous codons

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the spatial and temporal relationship of transcription and translation in prokaryotic cells versus eukaryotic cells.
back:
• Prokaryotes: Coupled (occur simultaneously in cytosol)
• Eukaryotes: Separated (Transcription in nucleus; Translation in cytoplasm)
• Eukaryotic mRNA requires extensive post-transcriptional processing

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Detail the specific enzyme and substrate required for the addition of the 3' poly-A tail in eukaryotic mRNA processing.
back:
• Enzyme: Polyadenylate polymerase
• Substrate: ATP
• Does not require a DNA template
• Enhances mRNA stability and translation efficiency

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: In bacterial transcription, the subunit of RNA polymerase necessary for identifying and binding the promoter sequence is the [___].
back:
• Sigma (σ) factor
• Required for initiation
• Converts core enzyme to holoenzyme
• Dissociates after the transcript exceeds ten nucleotides

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient ingests Amanita phalloides (death cap) mushrooms containing alpha-amanitin. Describe the primary effect on the central dogma.
back:
• Inhibits RNA Polymerase II
• Blocks eukaryotic mRNA synthesis
• Results in failure of protein production
• Leads to severe liver and kidney failure

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: How is transcription terminated in a Rho-independent (intrinsic) prokaryotic system?
back:
• Formation of a GC-rich hairpin (stem-loop)
• Followed by a string of Uracil residues
• Weak U-A binding causes RNA dissociation from DNA
• Termination occurs without additional protein factors

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between a nonsense mutation and a frameshift mutation in terms of the resulting polypeptide product.
back:
• Nonsense: Premature stop codon; produces truncated protein
• Frameshift: Insertion/deletion (not multiples of 3)
• Result: Radically different amino acid sequence downstream

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Name the enzyme responsible for charging tRNA with its specific amino acid and the high-energy molecule required for this process.
back:
• Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
• Energy Source: ATP
• Crucial for translational fidelity (proofreading activity)
• Links carboxyl group of amino acid to 3' CCA tail

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The flow of genetic information from a DNA template to a complementary RNA strand is a process termed [___].
back: * Transcription; * Catalyzed by RNA polymerase; * Proceeds in the 5' to 3' direction; * Primary site of gene regulation.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A victim of mushroom poisoning presents with severe hepatic failure due to alpha-amanitin. This toxin disrupts the central dogma by specifically targeting [___].
back: * RNA Polymerase II; * Prevents synthesis of mRNA; * Halts the production of protein-coding transcripts; * Results in systemic protein deficiency.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Outline the mechanism by which the "Wobble Hypothesis" allows a single tRNA species to recognize more than one codon.
back: * Flexible base pairing at the 3rd codon position; * Movement of the 5' anticodon base; * Recognizes synonymous codons; * Reduces the total tRNA species required.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the specific nucleotide sequences used for ribosome binding during translation initiation in prokaryotes versus eukaryotes.
back: * Prokaryotes: 16S rRNA binds the Shine-Dalgarno sequence; * Eukaryotes: 40S subunit recognizes the 5' 7-methylguanosine cap; * Prokaryotes use polycistronic templates; * Eukaryotes scan for the first AUG.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain how the addition of a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail preserves the integrity of the genetic message during its journey to the ribosome.
back: * Protects mRNA from nuclease degradation; * Facilitates export from the nucleus; * Increases translation initiation efficiency; * Enhances overall transcript stability.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: In the genetic code, a specific triplet of mRNA nucleotides that corresponds to a single amino acid or a termination signal is called a [___].
back: * Codon; * 61 codons specify amino acids; * 3 codons signal termination (Stop); * Read continuously in a 5' to 3' direction.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient is diagnosed with a genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the TATA box of a specific gene. Predict the most likely biochemical consequence regarding the central dogma.
back: * Failure of the transcription initiation complex to assemble; * Significantly reduced levels of mRNA; * Deficiency of the corresponding protein; * Disruption of basal gene expression.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Describe the molecular events mediated by the spliceosome that result in the conversion of hnRNA into mature mRNA.
back: * Identification of GU-AG consensus sequences; * Removal of non-coding introns as lariats; * Joining of expressed exons; * Facilitated by small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between missense and nonsense mutations in terms of their effect on the primary structure of the resulting polypeptide.
back: * Missense: Substitutes one amino acid for another; * Nonsense: Replaces a sense codon with a Stop codon; * Missense may alter protein function; * Nonsense leads to truncated proteins.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the family of enzymes responsible for the high-fidelity attachment of amino acids to their respective tRNA molecules.
back: * Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases; * Covalently links amino acids to the 3' CCA tail; * Requires ATP hydrolysis; * Possesses intrinsic proofreading (editing) activity.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The biological process describing the directional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and subsequently to protein is known as the [___].
back:
• Central Dogma
• DNA → RNA (Transcription)
• RNA → Protein (Translation)
• Exceptions include reverse transcription (RNA → DNA)

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A mutation occurs in the TATA box within the promoter region of a eukaryotic gene. Describe the primary effect on the central dogma in this patient.
back:
• Inhibits transcription initiation
• Prevents assembly of the preinitiation complex
• Reduces RNA polymerase II binding
• Decreased mRNA production leads to protein deficiency

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: How does RNA polymerase maintain the directionality of the central dogma during the transcription phase?
back:
• Reads DNA template 3' to 5'
• Synthesizes mRNA 5' to 3'
• Uses ribonucleoside triphosphates (ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP)
• No primer required for initiation

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the spatial and temporal relationship of transcription and translation in prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cells.
back:
• Prokaryotes: Coupled; translation begins before transcription finishes in the cytosol
• Eukaryotes: Spatially separated; transcription in nucleus, translation in cytoplasm
• Requires mRNA processing and nuclear export

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Summarize the energy requirements for adding a single amino acid to a growing polypeptide chain during translation.
back:
• Four high-energy bonds total
• Two from ATP (Aminoacyl-tRNA charging)
• One GTP for A-site binding
• One GTP for translocation step

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: During post-transcriptional modification, eukaryotic mRNA is stabilized by the addition of a [___] to the 5' end and a [___] to the 3' end.
back:
• 5' end: 7-methylguanosine cap
• 3' end: Poly-A tail
• Both facilitate translation and protect from nucleases

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A 1-year-old child presents with microcytic anemia due to a point mutation that creates a new splice acceptor site in the beta-globin gene. Explain the outcome.
back:
• Aberrant mRNA splicing
• Produces mRNA with extra/missing nucleotides
• Leads to frameshifts or truncated proteins
• Results in Beta-thalassemia

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Detail the role of the large ribosomal subunit in translating the genetic code into a functional protein.
back:
• Houses peptidyl transferase activity
• Catalyzes peptide bond formation (Ribozyme)
• Transfers peptide from P-site tRNA to A-site amino acid
• Mediates translocation of the ribosome

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Distinguish between the P-site and A-site functions within the ribosome during protein synthesis.
back:
• P-site (Peptidyl): Holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide chain
• A-site (Aminoacyl): Binds incoming charged tRNA specified by the mRNA codon
• E-site (Exit): Uncharged tRNA departs

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain the concept of 'degeneracy' in the genetic code and its importance for the central dogma.
back:
• Multiple codons specify one amino acid
• Minimizes the harmful effects of point mutations
• Usually involves 'wobble' at the third nucleotide
• Ensures translation remains robust

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA and then to protein is termed the [___].
back: * Central Dogma.* Proposed by Francis Crick.* Involves transcription (DNA to RNA) and translation (RNA to protein).

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: A patient diagnosed with tuberculosis is prescribed Rifampin. This medication inhibits the central dogma by targeting the [___] stage of gene expression.
back: * Transcription initiation.* Specifically binds to the beta subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase.* Prevents RNA chain growth beyond a few nucleotides.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Explain the mechanism by which eukaryotic cells protect mRNA from degradation and facilitate ribosomal binding at the 5' end.
back: * Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap.* Forms a 5'-to-5' triphosphate linkage.* Recognized by eIF-4 factors for translation initiation.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Contrast the functional consequence of alternative splicing versus RNA editing in the generation of protein diversity from a single gene.
back: * Alternative splicing: Joins different exon combinations.* RNA editing: Changes specific bases post-transcriptionally (e.g., Apo B-100 to B-48).* Both produce tissue-specific protein isoforms.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: Identify the role of the peptidyl transferase ribozyme during the elongation phase of translation.
back: * Located in the large ribosomal subunit.* Catalyzes peptide bond formation between amino acids.* Transfers the growing chain from P-site to A-site.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
front: The specific sequence on prokaryotic mRNA that correctly positions the small ribosomal subunit near the start codon is the [___].
back: * Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence.* Purine-rich region upstream of AUG.* Complementary to the 16S rRNA in the 30S subunit.

category: Discuss the concept of central dogma from gene to protein
