• S phase (Synthesis phase)
• Follows the G1 phase and precedes G2/Mitosis.
• Regulated by checkpoints involving cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Detail the fate of nucleosomes during the progression of the eukaryotic replication fork.
back:
• Parental nucleosomes are disassembled to allow access for helicase and polymerases.
• New nucleosomes reassemble rapidly on daughter strands behind the fork.
• Histones are derived from recycled parental units and de novo synthesis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish the enzyme responsible for replicating human mitochondrial DNA from the primary nuclear DNA polymerases.
back:
• Mitochondrial DNA: Replicated by DNA Polymerase gamma (γ).
• Nuclear DNA: Primarily Pol α, δ, and ε for synthesis.
• Mitochondrial replication resembles the prokaryotic circular system.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In eukaryotic replication, specify the location and frequency of RNA primer requirements on the leading versus lagging strands.
back:
• Leading strand: Requires only one primer at the origin for continuous synthesis.
• Lagging strand: Requires multiple primers, one for every Okazaki fragment.
• Primers are synthesized by the primase subunit of Pol α.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In eukaryotic cells, the specific enzyme responsible for the replication of mitochondrial DNA is [___].
back:
• DNA Polymerase ̲γ.
• It is a high-fidelity polymerase.
• Functionally independent of the nuclear replication machinery.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A child presents with signs of premature aging, including wrinkled skin and hair loss. Molecular analysis reveals significantly shortened chromosomal ends. What is the underlying pathophysiology?
back:
• Deficient Telomerase activity.
• Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein that maintains linear chromosome ends.
• Lack of repair leads to senescence after critical shortening.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain how the Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA) functions during eukaryotic DNA elongation.
back:
• Acts as a sliding DNA clamp.
• Increases the processivity of DNA polymerases ̲δ and ̲ε.
• Encircles the template to prevent enzyme dissociation.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the enzymatic mechanism of RNA primer removal in E. coli with that in human somatic cells.
back:
• Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I (5' to 3' exonuclease).
• Eukaryotes: RNase H and Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1).
• Eukaryotes do not utilize a polymerase for excision.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the dual enzymatic activities of the eukaryotic DNA Polymerase ̲α complex.
back:
• Possesses primase activity to start the RNA primer.
• Possesses 5' to 3' DNA polymerase activity.
• Synthesizes short iDNA segments before handing off to other polymerases.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In the eukaryotic cell cycle, the specific phase during which the entire genome undergoes semi-conservative replication is the [___] phase.
back:
• S phase (Synthesis phase).
• Occurs between G1 and G2 phases.
• Highly regulated by cyclins and CDKs.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A researcher observes that eukaryotic DNA strands re-anneal immediately after helicase action. A deficiency in which protein, functionally analogous to prokaryotic SSB, is likely present?
back:
• Replication Protein A (RPA).
• It binds and stabilizes single-stranded DNA.
• Protects templates from nuclease degradation.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe how eukaryotes achieve rapid replication of large genomes despite slower polymerase speeds than prokaryotes.
back:
• Utilization of multiple origins of replication per chromosome.
• Simultaneous synthesis at numerous replication bubbles.
• Contrast: Prokaryotes typically use a single origin (oriC).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish between the primary roles of eukaryotic DNA Polymerases ̲δ and ̲ε during fork progression.
back:
• Pol ̲ε: Synthesizes the continuous leading strand.
• Pol ̲δ: Synthesizes the discontinuous lagging strand (Okazaki fragments).
• Both possess 3' to 5' proofreading activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: State the fundamental difference in DNA topology that necessitates the use of telomerase in eukaryotes but not most prokaryotes.
back:
• Eukaryotic DNA is linear; prokaryotic DNA is usually circular.
• Linear ends (telomeres) cannot be fully replicated at the 3' end.
• Circular DNA lacks the "end-replication problem."

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In eukaryotic DNA replication, the polymerase primarily responsible for continuous synthesis on the leading strand is [___].
back:
• DNA Polymerase ε (epsilon).
• Highly processive enzyme.
• Possesses 3'→5' exonuclease activity for proofreading.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A laboratory analysis of malignant cells shows an unusual ability to maintain chromosomal length over many divisions. This immortal phenotype is due to the upregulated activity of [___].
back:
• Telomerase.
• An RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase).
• Adds TTAGGG repeats to the 3' ends of linear chromosomes to prevent senescence.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the functional role of the Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA) during the eukaryotic S-phase.
back:
• Acts as a sliding DNA clamp.
• Increases the processivity of DNA polymerases δ and ε.
• Encircles the DNA template to prevent the polymerase from dissociating.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the mechanism of RNA primer removal in E. coli with that in human cells.
back:
• Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I uses 5'→3' exonuclease activity.
• Eukaryotes: Primers are removed by RNase H and Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1).
• Eukaryotic polymerases (δ, ε) lack 5'→3' exonuclease activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the unique dual enzymatic activity of the Eukaryotic DNA Polymerase α complex.
back:
• Contains both primase and DNA polymerase activities.
• Synthesizes a short RNA primer followed by a ~20-nucleotide DNA 'initiator' strand.
• Lacks 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading) activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: The fundamental structural unit of eukaryotic chromatin, consisting of DNA wrapped around a core of eight basic proteins, is the [___].
back:
• Nucleosome.
• Core contains two molecules each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
• H1 binds the linker DNA to facilitate higher-order packing.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A patient with HIV is treated with Zidovudine (AZT). Why does this nucleoside analog cause chain termination during DNA synthesis?
back:
• AZT lacks a 3'-hydroxyl (-OH) group on its sugar moiety.
• Prevents the formation of the next 3'→5' phosphodiester bond.
• Successfully targets reverse transcriptase in viral replication.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Discuss why eukaryotic linear chromosomes require telomerase, whereas prokaryotic circular chromosomes do not.
back:
• The 'End-Replication Problem'.
• Lagging strand synthesis leaves a gap at the 5' end after primer removal.
• Circular DNA has no free ends, thus avoiding progressive shortening.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes regarding the number of origins of replication.
back:
• Prokaryotes: Single, unique origin (oriC).
• Eukaryotes: Multiple origins per chromosome.
• Multiple origins allow rapid replication of massive eukaryotic genomes despite slower polymerase speed.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In which phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle does semi-conservative DNA replication occur?
back:
• S-phase (Synthesis phase).
• Preceded by G1 (Gap 1) and followed by G2 (Gap 2).
• Regulated by checkpoints involving cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Unlike the single circular chromosome of prokaryotes, eukaryotic chromosomes utilize multiple [___] to facilitate the rapid replication of their extensive linear genomes.
back:
• Origins of replication
  • Increases efficiency for long DNA
  • Enables simultaneous synthesis at various points

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A laboratory analysis of senescent somatic cells shows progressively shorter chromosomal ends. In contrast, germ cells maintain their length using a ribonucleoprotein called [___].
back:
• Telomerase
  • Uses an internal RNA template (TERC)
  • Possesses reverse transcriptase activity (TERT)
  • Prevents the 'end-replication problem'

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the role of Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1) and RNase H in eukaryotic DNA replication.
back:
• Removal of RNA primers
  • Eukaryotic equivalent of Prokaryotic DNA Pol I exonuclease activity
  • Cleaves the RNA-DNA junction of Okazaki fragments

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the processivity factor Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA) with its functional equivalent in prokaryotic DNA replication.
back:
• PCNA (Eukaryotes) vs. Beta-subunit (Prokaryotes)
  • Both function as sliding DNA clamps
  • Encircle the template to prevent polymerase dissociation

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the specialized eukaryotic DNA polymerase that possesses intrinsic primase activity to initiate strand synthesis.
back:
• DNA Polymerase ̑ (Alpha)
  • Synthesizes a short RNA primer
  • Extends the primer with a small DNA segment (iDNA)
  • Lacks 3'-5' proofreading activity

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In the eukaryotic cell cycle, the strict temporal regulation of DNA synthesis ensures that replication occurs only during the [___] phase.
back:
• S (Synthesis) phase
  • Regulated by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks)
  • Preceded by G1 and followed by G2 phases

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 55-year-old patient with small cell lung cancer is treated with Irinotecan. Describe the specific eukaryotic enzyme targeted by this pharmacological agent.
back:
• Topoisomerase I
  • Relieves torsional strain by nicking a single strand
  • Inhibitors prevent DNA re-ligation, leading to double-strand breaks

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the dynamic fate of nucleosomes as the replication fork moves through eukaryotic chromatin.
back:
• Disassembled ahead of the fork
  • Rapidly reassembled on daughter strands
  • Utilizes both parental and newly synthesized histones
  • Mediated by histone chaperones

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the genomic templates used by DNA Polymerase ̕ (Epsilon) versus DNA Polymerase ̓ (Gamma).
back:
• Pol ̕: Synthesizes the leading strand in the nucleus
  • Pol ̓: Replicates circular mitochondrial DNA
  • Both exhibit high fidelity and proofreading

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the eukaryotic protein complex that serves as the single-stranded DNA binding protein, analogous to the prokaryotic SSB protein.
back:
• Replication Protein A (RPA)
  • Prevents re-annealing of separated strands
  • Protects ssDNA from nuclease degradation

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In eukaryotic DNA replication, the multisubunit enzyme that possesses both primase and DNA polymerase activity to initiate strand synthesis is [___].
back: DNA Polymerase alpha (Pol alpha); it synthesizes a short RNA primer followed by a short DNA segment; it notably lacks 3' to 5' exonuclease activity for proofreading.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 45-year-old patient is being studied for potential drug toxicity affecting cellular energy production. If the drug inhibits the specific eukaryotic enzyme responsible for replicating the circular mitochondrial genome, identify this polymerase.
back: DNA Polymerase gamma (Pol gamma); it is located exclusively in the mitochondria; it is responsible for the replication and repair of the circular mitochondrial genome.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the functional role of the Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA) during eukaryotic DNA elongation on the leading strand.
back: PCNA acts as a sliding DNA clamp; it encircles the DNA and tethers DNA Polymerase epsilon to the template; this significantly increases processivity for continuous leading-strand synthesis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Differentiate the prokaryotic and eukaryotic strategies for RNA primer removal, specifically addressing why eukaryotes require RNase H and FEN1.
back: Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I removes primers using 5' to 3' exonuclease activity. Eukaryotes: DNA polymerases lack this activity; they utilize RNase H and Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1) instead.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Specify the eukaryotic DNA polymerase primarily responsible for the synthesis and proofreading of Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
back: DNA Polymerase delta (Pol delta); it elongates the DNA segment initiated by Pol alpha; it possesses 3' to 5' exonuclease activity for high-fidelity proofreading.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Eukaryotic DNA replication is restricted to a specific phase of the cell cycle known as the [___].
back: S phase (Synthesis phase); it occurs between the G1 and G2 phases; it ensures the entire genome is replicated exactly once before mitosis begins.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A biopsy of aggressive malignant tissue shows increased telomere maintenance despite rapid division. Name the ribonucleoprotein responsible and describe how it extends chromosomal ends.
back: Telomerase; it uses its own internal RNA template to synthesize DNA at the 3' end of chromosomes; this prevents the 'end-replication problem' and cellular senescence.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the specific mechanism by which eukaryotic Topoisomerase II resolves the positive supercoiling induced by helicase at the replication fork.
back: It relieves torsional strain by making transient double-stranded breaks; it passes a second DNA segment through the break and reseals it; this process requires ATP hydrolysis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA regarding the number of origins of replication used during genomic duplication.
back: Prokaryotes utilize a single origin (oriC) on their circular chromosome. Eukaryotes utilize multiple origins per linear chromosome to facilitate rapid replication of their much larger genomes.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the group of basic, positively charged proteins that must be disassembled and rapidly reassembled into nucleosomes during eukaryotic DNA replication.
back: Histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4); these form an octameric core around which DNA wraps; their positive charge allows ionic bonding with the negatively charged DNA backbone.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
coreConcept: Eukaryotic Cell Cycle and DNA Replication
front: In eukaryotic cells, the specific phase of the cell cycle where the entire genome is duplicated is the [___] phase.
back:
• S phase (Synthesis phase)
• Follows G1 phase
• Precedes G2 phase and Mitosis
• Regulated by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks)

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A laboratory analysis of DNA replication identifies a multisubunit enzyme that possesses both primase and DNA polymerase activity. This enzyme is [___].
back:
• DNA Polymerase alpha (Pol α)
• Initiates strand synthesis on leading and lagging strands
• Synthesizes short RNA primer (~10 nt) followed by a short DNA segment (~20 nt)

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the biological necessity for eukaryotes to utilize multiple origins of replication per chromosome compared to the single origin in E. coli.
back:
• Large genome size: Eukaryotic DNA is significantly longer than prokaryotic DNA
• Speed: Multiple origins allow simultaneous replication to complete the process within the S phase duration

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the eukaryotic replication proteins PCNA and RPA with their functional prokaryotic homologs.
back:
• PCNA (Pro-Cellular Nuclear Antigen): Equivalent to Prokaryotic Beta-clamp (sliding clamp)
• RPA (Replication Protein A): Equivalent to Prokaryotic SSB (Single-Stranded Binding) proteins
• Both ensure high processivity and protect single strands

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
coreConcept: Division of Labor in Eukaryotic DNA Polymerases
front: Specify the division of labor between DNA Polymerase epsilon (ε) and DNA Polymerase delta (δ) at the replication fork.
back:
• Pol ε: Primarily responsible for continuous leading strand synthesis
• Pol δ: Primarily responsible for discontinuous lagging strand (Okazaki fragment) synthesis
• Both possess 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading activity

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: The enzyme required for the high-fidelity replication of circular mitochondrial DNA is [___].
back:
• DNA Polymerase gamma (Pol γ)
• Specifically located in mitochondria
• Possesses 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading activity
• Replicates the mitochondrial genome independently of nuclear DNA

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A patient presents with signs of premature cellular senescence. Molecular testing reveals a defect in a ribonucleoprotein that uses an internal RNA template to extend chromosomal ends. This enzyme is [___].
back:
• Telomerase
• Maintains chromosomal integrity at ends (telomeres)
• Contains TERT (Reverse Transcriptase) and TERC (RNA template)
• Prevents shortening of the G-rich strand during successive divisions

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the mechanism of RNA primer removal in eukaryotes, highlighting how it differs from the prokaryotic DNA Polymerase I mechanism.
back:
• Eukaryotes: Use RNase H and Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1) to excise primers
• Prokaryotes: Use 5'→3' exonuclease activity of DNA Polymerase I
• Eukaryotic DNA polymerases lack 5'→3' exonuclease activity

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
coreConcept: DNA Polymerase Beta vs Replicative Polymerases
front: Distinguish between the role of DNA Polymerase beta (Pol β) and the replicative polymerases (ε and δ).
back:
• Pol β: Involved in DNA repair (gap-filling during Base Excision Repair)
• Pol ε/δ: Involved in bulk genomic replication during S phase
• Pol β is not a primary replicative enzyme

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the structural complex that organizes eukaryotic DNA into 'beads on a string' to allow or inhibit replication access.
back:
• Nucleosome
• Composed of ~147 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4)
• Must be disassembled (chromatin remodeling) to allow replication fork progression

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Unlike the single circular chromosome of E. coli, eukaryotic DNA replication initiates at multiple sites along the linear chromosome known as [___].
back: - Origins of Replication (Replicons). - Facilitates rapid replication of large eukaryotic genomes. - Creates multiple bidirectional replication bubbles that eventually fuse.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 70-year-old patient's skin fibroblasts show significant chromosomal shortening after numerous divisions. This age-related senescence is prevented in germ cells by [___].
back: - Telomerase. - A ribonucleoprotein with reverse transcriptase activity. - Uses its own RNA template to extend the 3' ends of linear chromosomes. - Highly active in stem and cancer cells.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the dual enzymatic role of the DNA Polymerase α (alpha) complex during the initiation phase of eukaryotic replication.
back: - RNA Primase Activity: Synthesizes short RNA primers. - DNA Polymerase Activity: Extends the RNA with a short DNA segment (iDNA). - Lacks 3' to 5' exonuclease (proofreading) capability.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the mechanism of RNA primer removal on the lagging strand between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
back: - Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I removes primers using 5' to 3' exonuclease activity. - Eukaryotes: RNase H degrades RNA; Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1) removes the remaining displaced RNA/DNA 'flap'.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the eukaryotic protein that functions as a processivity factor by forming a sliding clamp, analogous to the β-subunit in E. coli.
back: - Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA). - Encircles DNA to hold polymerases δ and ε onto the template. - Essential for high-speed, continuous DNA synthesis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In the eukaryotic cell cycle, the specific phase during which DNA replication and histone synthesis occur is the [___].
back: - S-Phase (Synthesis Phase). - Follows the G1 checkpoint. - Precedes the G2 phase and mitosis (M-phase).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A patient with HIV is prescribed Zidovudine (AZT). Explain how this nucleoside analog inhibits DNA synthesis during replication.
back: - Lacks 3'-Hydroxyl (-OH) group: Prevents formation of the next 3'-5' phosphodiester bond. - Chain Termination: Acts as a substrate for reverse transcriptase and DNA polymerases. - Halts viral and host DNA elongation.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Detail the specific division of labor between DNA Polymerase δ (delta) and Polymerase ε (epsilon) at the eukaryotic replication fork.
back: - Polymerase ε: Primarily synthesizes the continuous leading strand. - Polymerase δ: Elongates the discontinuous Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand. - Both exhibit high fidelity via 3' to 5' proofreading.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish between the proteins used in prokaryotes and eukaryotes to stabilize single-stranded DNA and prevent re-annealing.
back: - Prokaryotes: Single-Stranded Binding (SSB) proteins. - Eukaryotes: Replication Protein A (RPA). - Both protect single-stranded DNA from nuclease degradation during synthesis.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Which eukaryotic DNA polymerase is unique for replicating extranuclear genetic material found in the mitochondria?
back: - DNA Polymerase γ (Gamma). - Responsible for the replication and repair of circular mitochondrial DNA. - Independent of nuclear DNA replication timing.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: The eukaryotic DNA polymerase primarily responsible for the elongation of the leading strand is [___].
back: * DNA polymerase epsilon (Pol ε).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 5-year-old child presents with multiple skin lesions and extreme sensitivity to UV light. This pathology is caused by a defect in the [___] system.
back: * Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER). * Specifically involves failure to remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the function of the RNA component (TERC) within the human telomerase enzyme complex.
back: * Acts as a template for synthesizing telomeric DNA. * Allows the reverse transcriptase component (TERT) to extend the 3' end of the chromosome.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the enzymatic mechanism for RNA primer removal in Escherichia coli versus human somatic cells.
back: * Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I removes primers via 5'-3' exonuclease activity. * Eukaryotes: Primers are excised by RNase H and Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the eukaryotic protein that functions as the sliding clamp to ensure the high processivity of DNA polymerases.
back: * Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In the eukaryotic cell cycle, the duplication of genomic DNA is restricted to the [___] phase.
back: * S phase (Synthesis phase).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A patient is treated with Zidovudine for a viral infection. Describe the biochemical reason this nucleoside analog acts as a chain terminator.
back: * It lacks the 3'-hydroxyl group required for phosphodiester bond formation. * Prevents further addition of nucleotides by DNA polymerase.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the coordinated action of DNA Polymerase alpha and the more processive eukaryotic polymerases during strand synthesis.
back: * Pol alpha/primase synthesizes a short RNA-DNA primer. * Synthesis is then handed off to Pol delta (lagging) or Pol epsilon (leading) for elongation.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish between the origin of replication sites in bacterial and human chromosomes.
back: * Prokaryotes: Single unique site (oriC). * Eukaryotes: Multiple origins per chromosome to facilitate rapid replication of large linear DNA molecules.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the protein complex in eukaryotes that binds to and stabilizes single-stranded DNA during the replication process.
back: * Replication Protein A (RPA).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: The eukaryotic protein functioning as a sliding DNA clamp to facilitate high processivity during the elongation phase is [___].
back: • PCNA (Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen). • Forms a ring that encircles the DNA. • Recruits Polymerase δ and ε to the template.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 5-year-old child presents with multiple hyperpigmented macules on sun-exposed areas and a biopsy confirms a basal cell carcinoma. This pathology most likely involves a defect in [___].
back: • Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER). • Failure to remove UV-induced pyrimidine (thymine) dimers. • Associated with Xeroderma Pigmentosum.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the specialized role of the DNA Polymerase α complex during the initiation of eukaryotic replication.
back: • Possesses primase activity to synthesize an RNA primer. • Exhibits 5'→3' polymerase activity to add a short DNA segment (iDNA). • Lacks 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the specific proteins required for the 'sliding clamp' and 'RNA primer removal' functions in eukaryotes versus prokaryotes.
back: • Sliding Clamp: PCNA (Eukaryotes) vs. β-subunit (Prokaryotes). • Primer Removal: RNase H and FEN1 (Eukaryotes) vs. DNA Polymerase I 5'→3' exonuclease (Prokaryotes).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the specific eukaryotic DNA polymerase that possesses 3'→5' exonuclease activity and is localized within the mitochondria.
back: • DNA Polymerase γ. • Responsible for replicating the circular mitochondrial genome. • Encoded by nuclear DNA.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In clinical flow cytometry, cells identified as having a DNA content between 2N and 4N are specifically in the [___] phase of the cell cycle.
back: • S phase (Synthesis phase). • The period where genomic DNA replication occurs. • Triggered by cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A laboratory study observes that a eukaryotic cell line replicates its entire genome in a fraction of the time required for E. coli, despite having a much larger genome. This is achieved through [___].
back: • Multiple origins of replication (replicons). • Simultaneous firing of origins across every chromosome. • Contrast to the single origin (oriC) in prokaryotes.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe the mechanism by which the telomerase complex prevents chromosomal shortening in germline and cancer cells.
back: • Uses an internal RNA template (TERC) to extend the 3' end of the G-rich strand. • Acts as an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase). • Maintains structural integrity of linear chromosome ends.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the functional roles of Eukaryotic DNA Polymerase δ and DNA Polymerase ε at the replication fork.
back: • Polymerase ε: Synthesizes the continuous leading strand. • Polymerase δ: Synthesizes the discontinuous lagging strand (Okazaki fragments). • Both utilize PCNA and have proofreading capabilities.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Name the structural complex that must be disassembled ahead of the replication fork and reassembled immediately after the DNA is synthesized.
back: • Nucleosome. • Consists of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4). • Requires ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: The eukaryotic DNA polymerase specifically responsible for replicating mitochondrial DNA is DNA Polymerase [___].
back:
• DNA Polymerase gamma (γ)
• It is a high-fidelity enzyme located exclusively in the mitochondria
• Essential for the maintenance of the mitochondrial genome.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 75-year-old patient's cells show a progressive loss of the hexameric sequence (AGGGTT) at the ends of chromosomes. This 'mitotic clock' mechanism is governed by the length of [___].
back:
• Telomeres
• These non-coding repeats protect chromosome ends from nuclease attack
• Their shortening beyond a critical length triggers cellular senescence.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the role of Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA) during the elongation phase of eukaryotic DNA replication.
back:
• Acts as a sliding DNA clamp
• Encircles the DNA strand to anchor DNA Polymerase delta (δ) or epsilon (ε)
• Significantly increases the processivity of the polymerase.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A researcher compares E. coli and human fibroblasts. Distinguish the proteins responsible for removing RNA primers in these two systems.
back:
• Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I (using its 5' to 3' exonuclease activity)
• Eukaryotes: RNase H and Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1)
• Both processes leave gaps later filled by DNA polymerases.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the eukaryotic protein complex that serves as the functional equivalent of the prokaryotic DnaB helicase.
back:
• MCM (Minichromosome Maintenance) complex
• It utilizes ATP to unwind the DNA double helix at the replication fork
• Part of the pre-replication complex.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In contrast to prokaryotic replication which occurs throughout the cell life, eukaryotic genomic DNA synthesis is strictly confined to the [___] phase.
back:
• S-phase (Synthesis phase)
• This period is preceded by G1 and followed by the G2 phase
• Regulated by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A patient with HIV is treated with Zidovudine (AZT). Describe why this nucleoside analog specifically prevents further DNA chain growth.
back:
• AZT is a thymidine analog lacking a 3'-hydroxyl (OH) group
• Once incorporated, it prevents the formation of 3'-to-5' phosphodiester bonds
• This leads to obligatory DNA chain termination.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Detail the mechanism of eukaryotic DNA packaging during replication to ensure genetic information is correctly condensed.
back:
• DNA wraps around an octameric core of histones to form nucleosomes
• Core consists of two molecules each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
• H1 histone binds the linker DNA to facilitate higher-order packing.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the number of origins of replication (ori) found in a typical bacterial chromosome versus a human chromosome.
back:
• Prokaryotes: Single, unique origin (oriC) per chromosome
• Eukaryotes: Multiple origins per chromosome
• Multiple sites allow the large eukaryotic genome to be replicated rapidly.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Which eukaryotic DNA polymerase is responsible for the continuous synthesis of the leading strand?
back:
• DNA Polymerase epsilon (ε)
• It possesses 5'-to-3' polymerase activity and 3'-to-5' exonuclease activity for proofreading
• Exhibits high processivity when associated with PCNA.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: At the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes, DNA is associated with a specialized protein complex called [___] that maintains structural integrity.
back: • Shelterin • Protects ends from nucleases • Prevents repair systems from mistaking ends as double-strand breaks.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A researcher observes that cultured human fibroblasts stop dividing after a specific number of population doublings. This phenomenon is known as [___].
back: • Senescence • Triggered when telomeres reach a critical minimum length • Acts as a tumor-suppressive mechanism in somatic cells.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain how the protein component TERT (Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase) functions during telomere maintenance.
back: • Acts as an RNA-directed DNA polymerase • Uses internal RNA (TERC) as a template • Extends the G-rich 3' overhang of the chromosome.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Telomeres in Somatic vs Cancer Cells
front: Distinguish between the telomere dynamics of normal human somatic cells and those of malignant cancer cells.
back: • Somatic: Telomeres shorten with each division; cells eventually senesce • Cancer: Telomerase is reactivated; telomere length is maintained, allowing immortality.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the component of the telomerase enzyme that provides the sequence for the hexameric repeats.
back: • TERC (Telomerase RNA Component) • Acts as the template for reverse transcription • Contains the sequence complementary to the AGGGTT repeats.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back: • AGGGTT • Base-paired to the AACCCT sequence • Leaves a single-stranded 3' overhang (G-rich strand).

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 5-year-old patient presents with symptoms of premature aging. Defective telomere maintenance is suspected. This group of disorders is collectively known as [___].
back: • Progerias (e.g., Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria) • Characterized by accelerated telomere shortening • Leads to early cell senescence and multi-system decline.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the role of DNA Polymerase alpha in completing the replication of telomeric ends after telomerase has acted.
back: • Uses the newly lengthened G-rich strand as a template • Synthesizes an RNA primer via its primase subunit • Extends the C-rich strand to fill the gap.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the G-rich strand and the C-rich strand of human telomeres regarding length and structure.
back: • G-rich: Longer 3' end, single-stranded overhang, forms loop structures • C-rich: Shorter 5' end, complementary to G-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: State why telomeres are often referred to as "mitotic clocks."
back: • Their length is inversely proportional to the number of cell divisions • Shortening marks the remaining proliferative lifespan of a cell.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In eukaryotic DNA replication, the multisubunit enzyme complex that possesses both primase and DNA polymerase activity to initiate strand synthesis is [___].
back:
**DNA Polymerase ̑ (alpha)**
• Initiates synthesis on leading and lagging strands.
• Synthesizes a short RNA primer followed by a 20-nucleotide DNA segment.
• Lacks 3’ to 5’ exonuclease proofreading activity.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A researcher identifies a cell line where DNA synthesis fails to occur due to an arrest at the G1/S checkpoint. This prevents the cell from entering the [___] phase of the cell cycle.
back:
**S (Synthesis) Phase**
• The specific window where DNA replication occurs.
• Regulated by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (Cdks).
• Distinct from prokaryotes where replication is not strictly phase-bound.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Explain the mechanism for RNA primer removal in eukaryotes and identify the key difference from the prokaryotic DNA Polymerase I system.
back:
**RNase H and FEN1 Mechanism**
• RNase H degrades the bulk of the RNA primer.
• Flap endonuclease 1 (FEN1) removes the final ribonucleotide.
• Prokaryotes utilize the 5' to 3' exonuclease activity of DNA Pol I.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the genomic origin of replication between prokaryotic circular chromosomes and eukaryotic linear chromosomes.
back:
**Single vs. Multiple Origins**
• Prokaryotes: Single unique site called oriC.
• Eukaryotes: Multiple origins per chromosome.
• Purpose: Enables rapid replication of massive eukaryotic genomes within a limited S-phase.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the primary eukaryotic polymerase responsible for leading-strand elongation and its associated sliding clamp protein.
back:
**DNA Polymerase ε (epsilon) and PCNA**
• Pol ε: High-fidelity replicase with 3' to 5' proofreading.
• PCNA (Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen): Eukaryotic sliding clamp.
• PCNA ensures high processivity of the enzyme.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: The specialized ribonucleoprotein that prevents chromosomal shortening in germ cells by utilizing its own RNA template for reverse transcription is [___].
back:
**Telomerase**
• Contains TERT (reverse transcriptase) and TERC (RNA template).
• Extends the 3’ G-rich overhanging end.
• Counteracts the ‘end-replication problem’ in linear chromosomes.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: An immunohistochemical stain for a biopsy specimen shows a high index of PCNA (Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen). Describe the pathophysiological significance of this marker in eukaryotic replication.
back:
**Cell Proliferation Marker**
• PCNA levels rise during S-phase to facilitate replication.
• High PCNA index indicates rapid cell division.
• Clinically used as a marker for malignancy/tumor growth rate.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Describe how eukaryotic cells manage the DNA-histone complex (nucleosome) as the replication fork advances.
back:
**Chromatin Remodeling**
• Nucleosomes are disassembled ahead of the fork.
• Rapidly reassembled on daughter strands behind the fork.
• Utilizes both recycled parental histones and newly synthesized ones.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Distinguish between the functional roles of eukaryotic DNA Polymerase δ (delta) and DNA Polymerase ε (epsilon).
back:
**Strand Specialization**
• Pol δ: Primarily elongates lagging strand (Okazaki fragments).
• Pol ε: Primarily elongates the leading strand.
• Both possess 3' to 5' exonuclease activity for high-fidelity proofreading.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Mention the specific structural feature of eukaryotic DNA that requires the enzyme telomerase for complete replication.
back:
**Linear Chromosome Ends**
• Eukaryotic DNA is linear (not circular like prokaryotes).
• Gap at the 5' end of the lagging strand cannot be filled.
• Telomerase prevents progressive loss of coding sequences.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: While E. coli uses a single unique consensus sequence, eukaryotic linear chromosomes utilize multiple [___] to ensure the entire genome is copied within the timeframe of the S-phase.
back:
• Origins of Replication (ori)
• Enables simultaneous synthesis at thousands of sites
• Coordinated by the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) to initiate melting.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A 5-year-old child presents with signs of premature aging. The pathophysiology involves the progressive shortening of [___] because DNA polymerase cannot fill the gap at the 5' end of the lagging strand.
back:
• Telomeres
• Tandem hexameric repeats (AGGGTT) at linear ends
• Protect chromosomes from nuclease attack and fusion
• Shortening leads to cellular senescence.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Contrast the primary catalytic roles of DNA Polymerase delta (δ) and DNA Polymerase epsilon (ε) during eukaryotic replication elongation.
back:
• Pol ε: Synthesizes the leading strand continuously
• Pol δ: Synthesizes the lagging strand (Okazaki fragments)
• Both exhibit 3'→5' exonuclease activity for high-fidelity proofreading.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: An experimental drug inhibits the enzyme FEN1 (Flap Endonuclease 1). Contrast the expected impact on eukaryotic lagging strand maturation with the prokaryotic mechanism for primer removal.
back:
• Eukaryotes: FEN1 and RNase H cooperate to remove RNA/DNA flaps
• Prokaryotes: DNA Polymerase I removes primers via 5'→3' exonuclease
• Result: Inhibition causes accumulation of unligated Okazaki fragments.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Identify the pharmacological mechanism by which nucleoside analogs like Cytarabine (araC) inhibit the S-phase of the cell cycle during cancer chemotherapy.
back:
• Chain termination
• Analog is converted to a nucleotide and incorporated into DNA
• Lack of a proper 3'-OH group prevents further phosphodiester bond formation.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: In the laboratory assessment of proliferating cells, the marker used to identify active DNA replication sites due to its role as the eukaryotic sliding clamp is [___].
back:
• PCNA (Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen)
• Enhances processivity of DNA polymerases by encircling the DNA
• Loaded onto the template by Replication Factor C (RFC).

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: A patient with a metabolic disorder exhibits hypoacetylation of histones. Apply your knowledge of chromatin remodeling to explain the likely effect on DNA replication initiation.
back:
• Chromatin remains in a condensed (heterochromatin) state
• Positive charges on histones bind DNA tightly
• Reduces access for the Origin Recognition Complex and helicases.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Differentiate the termination of DNA replication in eukaryotes from the protein-mediated arrest mechanism utilized by prokaryotes like E. coli.
back:
• Eukaryotes: Forks simply collide and are ligated along linear DNA
• Prokaryotes: Sequence-specific Ter sites bind Tus protein to stop forks
• Eukaryotic ends (telomeres) require telomerase for length maintenance.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
coreConcept: Replication Licensing and the Cell Cycle
front: Describe the physiological loop between Cyclin-Dependent Kinases (CDKs) and the MCM helicase complex that prevents DNA over-replication.
back:
• G1 Phase: Low CDK allows ORC/Cdc6/Cdt1 to load (license) MCM
• S Phase: High CDK activates MCM to initiate unwinding
• Regulation: Active CDKs simultaneously inhibit re-licensing until mitosis is complete.

category: Describe in detail all the steps in Eukaryotic DNA replication with emphasis on differences between Pro- and Eukaryotes
front: Specify the role of Replication Protein A (RPA) in the eukaryotic replication fork and identify its prokaryotic functional equivalent.
back:
• Role: Binds single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) to prevent re-annealing
• Protection: Shields ssDNA from nuclease degradation
• Equivalent: Single-Stranded Binding (SSB) protein in prokaryotes.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The specialized ribonucleoprotein enzyme responsible for maintaining chromosomal length in germ cells and stem cells is [___].
back:
• Telomerase
• Consists of TERT (protein) and TERC (RNA)
• Prevents replicative senescence

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A biopsy of a malignant tumor reveals cells that divide indefinitely. The enzyme upregulated in these cells to prevent 'mitotic clock' exhaustion is [___].
back:
• Telomerase
• Acts as a reverse transcriptase
• Facilitates cellular immortality in 90% of cancers

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the TERC component during the extension of telomeric DNA.
back:
• Acts as an internal RNA template
• Base pairs with the G-rich 3' overhang
• Provides the sequence (AACCCT) for DNA synthesis

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Somatic vs. Stem Cell Telomere Dynamics
front: A 75-year-old patient's fibroblasts show shortened chromosomal ends, whereas their hematopoietic stem cells maintain length. Explain this disparity.
back:
• Somatic cells lack telomerase; telomeres shorten per division
• Stem cells express telomerase; maintain telomere length
• Shortening in somatic cells leads to senescence

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the specific biochemical activity of the TERT subunit of telomerase.
back:
• RNA-directed DNA polymerase
• Functionally a reverse transcriptase
• Synthesizes DNA in the 5' to 3' direction

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, the noncoding hexameric tandem repeat sequence found at the 3' end of telomeres is [___].
back:
• AGGGTT
• Repeats several thousand times
• Forms a protective loop structure

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A laboratory-grown cell line reaches its limit of division and enters a non-dividing but viable state. This state is triggered by [___].
back:
• Critical telomere shortening
• Known as replicative senescence
• Acts as a biological tumor-suppressor mechanism

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: How do telomeres prevent double-strand break (DSB) repair systems from attacking the ends of linear chromosomes?
back:
• Form T-loops via 3' overhang folding
• Associated with 'Shelterin' protein complex
• Masks DNA ends from being recognized as breaks

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the 'G-rich strand' and 'C-rich strand' of a human telomere regarding length and structure.
back:
• G-rich strand: 3' end, longer overhang, AGGGTT repeats
• C-rich strand: 5' end, shorter, AACCCT repeats
• G-overhang is essential for telomerase binding

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the protein complex that organizes telomeric DNA into a protective cap and regulates telomerase access.
back:
• Shelterin
• Prevents nucleolytic attack
• Distinguishes true chromosomal ends from DNA damage

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Human telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back:
• AGGGTT (paired with AACCCT)
• The G-rich strand is longer, creating a 3' single-stranded overhang
• This sequence is added by telomerase to prevent genetic loss.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A researcher notes that malignant cells avoid senescence despite hundreds of divisions. This cellular 'immortality' is primarily due to the upregulation of the ribonucleoprotein [___].
back:
• Telomerase
• It maintains telomere length, preventing the mitotic clock from triggering apoptosis
• Highly active in germ, stem, and cancer cells.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the enzymatic mechanism by which telomerase extends chromosomal ends.
back:
• It is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase
• TERC (RNA) provides the template
• TERT (protein) acts as reverse transcriptase to extend the 3' G-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast telomere dynamics in normal human somatic cells with those in germline cells.
back:
• Somatic: Telomeres shorten each division; leads to senescence/aging
• Germline: Telomerase is active; length is maintained allowing indefinite division.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the two essential components of the human telomerase complex and their specific functions.
back:
• TERC: An RNA molecule that serves as the template for repeats
• TERT: A protein acting as reverse transcriptase to synthesize DNA.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In most human tissues, telomeres are often described as [___] because their length is inversely related to the number of times a cell has divided.
back:
• Mitotic Clocks
• Critical shortening triggers cellular senescence
• This process limits the lifespan of somatic cell lineages.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 12-year-old child presents with features of premature aging (progeria). The underlying biochemical defect involves accelerated shortening of [___].
back:
• Telomeres
• Loss of chromosomal end-protection leads to early cell death
• Associated with defects in telomere maintenance proteins.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the specific 'end-replication problem' faced by eukaryotic cells during lagging strand synthesis.
back:
• RNA primer removal at the 5' end leaves a gap
• DNA polymerase cannot fill this gap (no 3'-OH available)
• Results in progressive chromosomal shortening.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the G-rich and C-rich strands of human telomeres regarding their length.
back:
• G-rich strand: Longer strand; features the 3' single-stranded overhang
• C-rich strand: Shorter complementary strand; synthesized by DNA polymerase alpha.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the specific protein complex that coats telomeres to prevent them from being recognized as double-strand breaks.
back:
• Shelterin
• It hides the chromosome ends from nucleases
• Prevents inappropriate DNA repair/ligation of chromosomal ends.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In human chromosomes, the noncoding hexameric sequence that is tandemly repeated at the telomeres is [___].
back:
• AGGGTT (on the G-rich strand).
• It is base-paired to the complementary AACCCT sequence.
• These repeats form the protective ends of linear DNA.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Biopsy of a malignant tumor reveals cells that can divide indefinitely without entering senescence. This 'immortality' is primarily achieved by the upregulation of which ribonucleoprotein?
back:
• Telomerase.
• It maintains telomere length, preventing the critical shortening that normally triggers cell death or senescence in somatic cells.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the specific role of the RNA component (TERC) within the telomerase enzyme complex.
back:
• It acts as a template for DNA synthesis.
• Its sequence (AACCCT) base-pairs with the G-rich 3' overhang of the telomere to guide extension.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the physiological fate of telomeres in normal somatic cells versus germline/stem cells during successive replicative cycles.
back:
• Somatic cells: Telomeres shorten with each division, leading to eventual senescence.
• Germline/Stem cells: Telomerase maintains length, allowing continuous division without loss of structural integrity.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the protein component of telomerase and name its specific enzymatic activity.
back:
• TERT (Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase).
• Activity: RNA-directed DNA polymerase (Reverse Transcriptase).
• It extends the 3' end of the G-rich telomeric strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The protective protein complex that associates with telomeric DNA to stabilize the loop structure and prevent nuclease attack is known as [___].
back:
• Shelterin.
• It shields the 3' single-stranded overhang from being recognized as a double-stranded DNA break by repair systems.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 5-year-old child presents with features of premature aging, including skin wrinkling and hair loss. Laboratory tests indicate significantly shortened telomeres for the patient's age. This clinical picture is characteristic of [___].
back:
• Progeria (e.g., Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome).
• It involves defective telomere maintenance or accelerated shortening, leading to premature cellular senescence and tissue aging.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the 'end-replication problem' that necessitates the presence of telomerase in eukaryotes.
back:
• DNA polymerase cannot fill the gap at the extreme 5' end of the lagging strand.
• Removal of the final RNA primer leaves no 3'-OH for extension, causing progressive shortening.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the G-rich strand and the C-rich strand regarding their length and structural orientation at the chromosomal terminus.
back:
• G-rich strand: Longer, contains AGGGTT repeats, and forms a 3' single-stranded overhang.
• C-rich strand: Shorter, contains AACCCT repeats, and is base-paired to the G-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Briefly define the concept of telomeres acting as a 'mitotic clock.'
back:
• Telomere length is inversely proportional to the number of times a cell has divided.
• It serves as a biomarker for biological aging and replicative capacity.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In human chromosomes, the noncoding hexameric sequence that is repeated thousands of times at the telomeric ends is [___].
back:
• **AGGGTT** (or TTAGGG)
• Repeated in tandem to form the G-rich strand
• Paired with a complementary C-rich strand (AACCCT)

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A biopsy of a malignant tumor reveals cells that bypass the normal limit of cell division, exhibiting "immortality." This clinical feature is primarily due to the upregulation of [___].
back:
• **Telomerase**
• Maintains telomere length
• Prevents replicative senescence seen in somatic cells

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the RNA component (TERC) within the telomerase ribonucleoprotein complex.
back:
• Acts as a **template** for DNA synthesis
• Base-pairs with the single-stranded 3' end of telomeric DNA
• Guides the reverse transcriptase (TERT) during elongation

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the activity of telomerase in normal human somatic cells versus germ cells and stem cells.
back:
• **Somatic cells**: Low/absent activity; telomeres shorten until senescence
• **Germ/Stem cells**: High activity; telomere length is maintained
• Somatic cells act as a "mitotic clock"

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the specific enzymatic activity of the TERT protein component of telomerase.
back:
• **Reverse Transcriptase** activity
• Synthesizes DNA (5'→3') using an RNA template
• Specifically extends the longer G-rich 3' end

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Telomeric DNA is protected from nuclease attack and recognized as a true chromosome end rather than a break by a protein complex called [___].
back:
• **Shelterin**
• Stabilizes the loop structure formed by the G-rich strand
• Maintains structural integrity of the chromosome

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A child presents with signs of accelerated physical aging and hair loss. This group of disorders, known as progerias, is biochemically linked to [___].
back:
• **Premature shortening of telomeres**
• Rapid onset of cellular senescence
• Failure of telomere maintenance mechanisms

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Synthesis of the C-rich Telomeric Strand
front: Describe the mechanism by which the 'C-rich' strand of the telomere is synthesized after telomerase has extended the 'G-rich' strand.
back:
• **DNA Polymerase α** (alpha) provides primase activity
• Synthesizes an RNA primer using the G-rich strand as a template
• Primer is extended and then removed by nucleases

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the terms 'senescence' and 'immortality' in the context of telomere dynamics.
back:
• **Senescence**: Growth arrest when telomeres reach a critical short length
• **Immortality**: Indefinite division due to telomere maintenance (typical of cancer/germ cells)

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Why is the linear nature of eukaryotic chromosomes problematic for DNA Polymerase during replication?
back:
• **End-replication problem**
• Removal of the 5' end RNA primer on the lagging strand leaves a gap
• No 3'-OH available to fill the terminal gap with DNA

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The protein component of the telomerase complex that functions as a reverse transcriptase to extend chromosomal ends is known as [___].
back:
• TERT (Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase).
• Function: Uses an internal RNA template to synthesize DNA.
• Direction: 5' to 3' extension of the G-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A biopsy of a malignant tumor reveals cells that divide indefinitely without experiencing senescence. This 'immortality' is primarily achieved through the up-regulation of [___].
back:
• Telomerase.
• Pathophysiology: Prevents the critical shortening of telomeres.
• Clinical Correlation: Active in cancer, germ, and stem cells; inactive in most somatic cells.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain why linear eukaryotic chromosomes shorten at the 5' end of the lagging strand during every round of DNA replication.
back:
• End-Replication Problem: Removal of the extreme 5' RNA primer leaves a gap.
• DNA polymerase cannot fill this gap as it requires a 3'-OH upstream.
• Result: Progressive loss of telomeric sequences.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 5-year-old child presents with features of premature aging (progeria). Contrast the telomerase activity in this child's somatic cells with that found in malignant cells.
back:
• Progeria: Accelerated telomere shortening or defective maintenance.
• Malignant Cells: High telomerase activity maintains telomere length.
• Outcome: Malignant cells avoid senescence, while progeria cells undergo premature cell death.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the specific role of the TERC component within the telomerase ribonucleoprotein complex.
back:
• TERC (Telomerase RNA Component).
• Function: Acts as an intrinsic RNA template.
• Sequence: Contains a sequence complementary to the telomeric repeats (e.g., AACCCT).

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Human telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back:
• 5'-AGGGTT-3'.
• Structure: Paired to the complementary AACCCT sequence.
• Feature: The G-rich strand is longer, leaving a 3' single-stranded overhang.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A researcher notes that as adult somatic cells age, they eventually enter a state called 'senescence.' This biological state is triggered when [___].
back:
• Telomeres reach a critical threshold length.
• Mechanism: The shortened ends are recognized as DNA damage.
• Clinical Term: Often called the 'Hayflick limit' or 'Mitotic Clock.'

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the structural mechanism by which the single-stranded 3' end of telomeric DNA prevents chromosomal instability.
back:
• T-loop formation: The overhang folds back on itself.
• Shelterin complex: Specialized proteins stabilize this loop.
• Function: Masks the chromosome end from nucleases and DNA repair machinery.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the templates used by DNA Polymerase delta (δ) and Telomerase during eukaryotic DNA synthesis.
back:
• DNA Polymerase δ: Uses the parental DNA strand as a template.
• Telomerase: Uses its own internal RNA molecule (TERC) as a template.
• Similarity: Both synthesize DNA in the 5' to 3' direction.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the clinical significance of telomeres in the context of human aging.
back:
• Mitotic Clock: Telomere length is inversely related to the number of cell divisions.
• Tissue Atrophy: Shortening leads to senescence and reduced regenerative capacity.
• Longevity: Associated with the biology of normal aging and progerias.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, the specialized complexes at the ends of linear chromosomes that consist of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___] are known as telomeres.
back:
• AGGGTT
• Base-paired to the complementary AACCCT sequence
• Protects chromosomal ends from nucleases and fusion

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A laboratory study observes that human somatic cells stop dividing after a fixed number of replications. This "mitotic clock" phenomenon is primarily driven by the progressive shortening of [___].
back:
• Telomeres
• Shortening occurs due to the "end replication problem"
• Leads to cellular senescence once a critical length is reached

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the RNA component (TERC) within the telomerase complex during the elongation of chromosomal ends.
back:
• Acts as a built-in template for DNA synthesis
• Base-pairs with the single-stranded 3' overhang
• Provides the sequence used by the TERT protein for extension

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the telomere maintenance capacity between mature human somatic cells and malignant neoplastic cells.
back:
• Somatic: Lack telomerase; telomeres shorten, leading to senescence
• Neoplastic: Telomerase is reactivated; maintains telomere length
• Result: Cancer cells achieve replicative immortality

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the specialized protein complex that associates with telomeric DNA to prevent it from being recognized as a double-stranded DNA break.
back:
• Shelterin
• Stabilizes the protective T-loop structure
• Prevents inappropriate activation of DNA repair pathways

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The catalytic protein component of telomerase (TERT) functions biochemically as a(n) [___], which is essential for maintaining germline and stem cell longevity.
back:
• Reverse transcriptase (RNA-directed DNA polymerase)
• Synthesizes DNA in the 5'→3' direction using an RNA template
• Specifically extends the G-rich 3' overhang

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A child presents with skin hyperpigmentation, nail dystrophy, and bone marrow failure. Molecular analysis reveals defective telomere maintenance. Identify the most likely affected enzymatic process.
back:
• Telomerase activity
• Consistent with Dyskeratosis Congenita
• Resulting in premature cellular aging and stem cell depletion

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain why the 5' end of the lagging strand cannot be fully replicated in eukaryotic linear chromosomes.
back:
• Removal of the terminal RNA primer leaves a gap
• DNA polymerase requires a 3'-OH group for extension
• No upstream primer exists to provide that group

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the TERT and TERC subunits of the telomerase holoenzyme based on their biochemical nature.
back:
• TERT: The protein subunit (Reverse Transcriptase enzyme)
• TERC: The RNA subunit (Template for synthesis)
• Both form the functional ribonucleoprotein complex

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: State the structural significance of the single-stranded G-rich 3' overhang found at the end of eukaryotic chromosomes.
back:
• Folds back into the double-strand to form a T-loop
• Provides the attachment site for telomerase enzyme
• Stabilized by shelterin to hide the DNA end

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back:
• AGGGTT (G-rich strand).
• It maintains structural integrity of linear chromosomes.
• Prevents nucleolytic attack and distinguishes true ends from DNA breaks.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Most normal human somatic cells stop dividing after a fixed number of cycles. This 'mitotic clock' is fundamentally driven by the progressive shortening of [___].
back:
• Telomeres.
• Caused by the 'end-replication problem' on the lagging strand.
• When critical length is lost, the cell enters senescence.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the biochemical role of the TERT and TERC components of the telomerase complex.
back:
• TERT: The protein subunit acting as a reverse transcriptase.
• TERC: The RNA subunit providing the template (AACCCT).
• Together they extend the 3' end of chromosomal DNA.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the activity of telomerase in normal adult somatic cells with that observed in malignant cancer cells.
back:
• Somatic cells: Negligible activity; telomeres shorten, leading to cell death.
• Cancer cells: High activity (90% of cases); telomere length is maintained, conferring replicative immortality.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the specific enzymatic classification of telomerase based on its template and product.
back:
• RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.
• Also known as a specialized reverse transcriptase.
• Uses its internal RNA to direct DNA synthesis.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The protein complex that protects the G-rich single-stranded 3' overhang of telomeres by facilitating loop formation is known as [___].
back:
• Shelterin.
• It prevents DNA repair machinery from recognizing chromosome ends as double-strand breaks.
• Essential for telomere stability.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A patient presents with features of premature aging (progeria). This pathology is molecularly associated with accelerated [___].
back:
• Telomere shortening.
• Limited proliferative capacity of cells causes early tissue dysfunction.
• Represents a failure in telomere maintenance mechanisms.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the structural mechanism of the 'loop' formation at the terminal ends of eukaryotic chromosomes.
back:
• The single-stranded G-rich 3' overhang folds back on itself.
• It base pairs with the double-stranded telomeric region.
• This 'caps' the DNA to prevent exonuclease digestion.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the fate of telomeres in germ cells versus adult fibroblasts.
back:
• Germ cells: High telomerase activity maintains length across generations.
• Adult fibroblasts: Low/no telomerase; telomeres shorten by ~50-200 bps per division cycle.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: State the primary reason why DNA polymerase cannot replicate the extreme 5' end of the lagging strand.
back:
