• Removal of the terminal RNA primer leaves a gap.
• No 3'-OH group is available for DNA polymerase to extend.
• Termed the 'end-replication problem.'

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back:
• AGGGTT
• Base-paired to the complementary AACCCT sequence.
• Prevents nucleolytic attack and double-strand break recognition.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with metastatic adenocarcinoma. Biopsy reveals malignant cells that avoid senescence despite rapid division. This cellular immortality is primarily due to the upregulation of [___].
back:
• Telomerase
• This ribonucleoprotein maintains telomere length.
• Prevents the 'mitotic clock' from reaching critical shortening that triggers senescence.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Differentiate between the roles of the TERT and TERC components of the telomerase complex.
back:
• TERT: A protein acting as a reverse transcriptase to synthesize DNA.
• TERC: A short RNA molecule serving as the template for the synthesis of G-rich repeats.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the telomere dynamics of normal human somatic cells with those of germline and hematopoietic stem cells.
back:
• Somatic cells: Telomeres shorten with each division; eventually lead to senescence.
• Germline/Stem cells: Telomerase is active; length is maintained allowing indefinite proliferative capacity.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Detail the 'End Replication Problem' that necessitates the presence of telomeres in linear eukaryotic chromosomes.
back:
• Standard DNA polymerases require a 3'-OH primer.
• Removal of the 5'-terminal RNA primer on the lagging strand leaves a gap that cannot be filled.
• Results in progressive chromosome shortening.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The specialized protein complex that protects the single-stranded 3' end of telomeres and stabilizes the loop structure is known as [___].
back:
• Shelterin
• Allows repair systems to distinguish true chromosome ends from double-strand breaks.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A researcher observes a group of cells where telomeres are abnormally short for the patient's age. This cellular phenotype is a hallmark of [___].
back:
• Progerias (Premature aging syndromes)
• Normal aging is also characterized by progressive telomere shortening in somatic tissues.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe how the complementary 'C-rich' strand is synthesized after telomerase has extended the 'G-rich' strand.
back:
• Telomerase extends the 3' overhang (G-rich).
• Primase activity of DNA polymerase α then synthesizes an RNA primer.
• DNA polymerase α extends the primer to fill the gap on the C-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the structural configurations of the G-rich and C-rich strands at the terminal end of a chromosome.
back:
• G-rich strand: Longer; terminates in a single-stranded 3' overhang.
• C-rich strand: Shorter; paired with the internal portion of the G-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: State the correlation between telomere length and the biological 'mitotic clock' in aging cells.
back:
• Inverse correlation: As divisions increase, telomere length decreases.
• Critical shortening triggers cellular senescence (permanent exit from the cell cycle).

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, the repetitive noncoding hexameric sequence found at the terminal ends of linear chromosomes is [___].
back:
• TTAGGG (on the G-rich strand).
• Repeated several thousand times.
• Base-paired to the AACCCT sequence.
• Forms a protective loop structure stabilized by shelterin proteins.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Malignant cells often bypass the Hayflick limit and achieve "immortality" by upregulating which specific ribonucleoprotein?
back:
• Telomerase.
• Maintains telomere length despite rapid division.
• Prevents the mitotic clock from triggering senescence or apoptosis.
• Target for potential anti-cancer therapeutics.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of TERC within the telomerase enzyme complex during DNA extension.
back:
• Acts as an essential RNA template.
• Provides the sequence for the hexameric repeats.
• Base-pairs with the 3'-overhang of the G-rich telomeric strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the catalytic TERT subunit with the TERC subunit of the telomerase complex.
back:
• TERT: The protein component; acts as a reverse transcriptase (RNA-directed DNA polymerase).
• TERC: The RNA component; provides the internal template for synthesis.
• TERT synthesizes DNA in the 5'→3' direction.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the physiological "End-Replication Problem" encountered by linear eukaryotic chromosomes.
back:
• Occurs on the lagging strand.
• Removal of the terminal RNA primer leaves a gap.
• DNA polymerase cannot fill the 5' end without a 3'-OH.
• Results in progressive chromosomal shortening each division.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Normal human somatic cells that can no longer divide due to critically short telomeres are biologically described as [___].
back:
• Senescent.
• Occurs once telomeres reach a critical threshold length.
• Represents a mitotic clock linked to cellular aging and the Hayflick limit.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A child presents with skin wrinkling and premature aging features. How does telomere biology explain the pathogenesis of such progeria syndromes?
back:
• Accelerated telomere shortening.
• Caused by defects in DNA repair or shelterin proteins.
• Early onset of cellular senescence leads to premature tissue exhaustion and aging phenotypes.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Detail the steps by which the C-rich strand is completed after telomerase has extended the G-rich strand.
back:
• Extended G-rich strand acts as a template.
• DNA polymerase alpha (pol α) is recruited.
• Primase subunit synthesizes an RNA primer.
• DNA pol α extends the primer to fill the gap.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between telomerase expression in human germ cells versus mature somatic cells.
back:
• Germ/Stem Cells: High telomerase activity; maintains full-length chromosomes for the next generation.
• Mature Somatic Cells: Low or absent activity; telomeres shorten with every mitotic cycle.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the multi-protein complex that stabilizes the telomeric T-loop and prevents its recognition as a double-strand break.
back:
• Shelterin.
• Sequesters the single-stranded 3' end.
• Protects terminal DNA from nuclease degradation and inappropriate DNA repair mechanisms.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In human chromosomes, telomeres consist of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back:
• TTAGGG.
• These sequences are base-paired to an AACCCT strand.
• They feature a single-stranded G-rich overhang at the 3' end.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Cellular Senescence and the Mitotic Clock
front: A 75-year-old male's fibroblasts show significantly reduced division capacity compared to a newborn's. This 'senescence' is triggered when [___] reach a critical minimum length.
back:
• Telomeres.
• In most somatic cells, telomeres shorten with each division.
• This occurs because DNA polymerase cannot fill the gap left by the final RNA primer.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the two essential components of the telomerase complex and their respective biological roles.
back:
• TERT: A protein acting as a reverse transcriptase (RNA-directed DNA polymerase).
• TERC: A short RNA molecule serving as the template for synthesizing telomeric DNA repeats.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast telomere dynamics in normal adult somatic cells with those found in germline and malignant cancer cells.
back:
• Somatic Cells: Lack telomerase; telomeres shorten progressively leading to senescence.
• Germ/Cancer Cells: Express telomerase, which maintains telomere length, conferring 'immortality' and infinite replicative potential.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the primary function of the 'shelterin' protein complex associated with chromosomal ends.
back:
• Protects chromosome ends from degradation by nucleases.
• Prevents DNA repair systems from mistakenly identifying telomeres as double-stranded breaks (DSBs).

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Telomerase is categorized as an [___]-directed DNA polymerase because it uses an internal sequence to extend the 3' end of the G-rich strand.
back:
• RNA-directed.
• It utilizes its own RNA component (TERC) as a template to add TTAGGG repeats to the existing DNA strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of Telomeres in Progeria
front: A 5-year-old child presents with thin skin, alopecia, and atherosclerosis. If accelerated telomere attrition is suspected, how does this explain the clinical phenotype?
back:
• Suggests a Progeria (premature aging syndrome).
• Rapid telomere shortening causes cells to enter senescence early.
• This severely limits tissue regenerative capacity and mimics advanced aging.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the 'T-loop' structure formed at the 3' end of human chromosomes.
back:
• The 3' G-rich overhang folds back and invades the double-stranded DNA.
• This sequesters the free end, masking it from DNA damage sensors and exonucleases.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the roles of DNA Polymerase α and Telomerase during the maintenance of chromosomal ends.
back:
• Telomerase: Extends the 3' end of the G-rich strand using an RNA template.
• DNA Pol α: Uses primase activity to synthesize a primer for filling the complementary C-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the specific biochemical reason telomeres are essential for linear, but not circular, DNA molecules.
back:
• Linear DNA faces the 'end-replication problem' where the 5' end cannot be fully replicated.
• Circular DNA (prokaryotic) has no ends and thus does not require telomeres.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back:
* AGGGTT.
* It is base-paired to the repeating AACCCT sequence.
* The G-rich strand is longer, forming a 3' single-stranded overhang.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A biopsy of a malignant tumor reveals cells that divide indefinitely without entering senescence. This replicative immortality is primarily due to the upregulated activity of [___].
back:
* Telomerase.
* It maintains telomere length despite repeated divisions.
* In contrast, normal somatic cells lack significant telomerase activity and eventually undergo senescence.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the two primary components (TERT and TERC) of the telomerase complex during DNA extension.
back:
* TERC: An RNA molecule that provides the template for DNA synthesis.
* TERT: A protein acting as a reverse transcriptase (RNA-directed DNA polymerase).
* Together, they extend the 3' end of the G-rich strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 5-year-old child presents with features of premature aging, including graying hair and skin atrophy. Contrast the state of the 'mitotic clock' in this patient with a healthy age-matched peer.
back:
* Patient has accelerated telomere shortening.
* Cells reach the critical length (Hayflick limit) earlier.
* This leads to premature senescence and the clinical phenotype of progeria.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the 'end-replication problem' that occurs at the 5' end of the lagging strand in eukaryotes.
back:
* DNA polymerase requires a 3'-OH primer for synthesis.
* Removal of the terminal RNA primer leaves a gap.
* No upstream 3'-OH exists to fill this gap, leading to progressive shortening.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Telomeres are considered [___] because their length in most cells is inversely related to the number of times the cell has divided.
back:
* Mitotic clocks.
* Shortening beyond a critical length prevents further division.
* This signals the cell to enter the senescent state.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Laboratory analysis of hematopoietic stem cells shows high telomerase activity compared to skin fibroblasts. Predict the impact of this activity on stem cell longevity.
back:
* Telomerase maintains telomere length during division.
* This prevents senescence and allows for unlimited proliferative capacity.
* It is essential for constant replenishment of blood cell populations.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the expected telomere dynamics and enzymatic activity in a normal human fibroblast versus a HeLa (cancer) cell line after 100 population doublings.
back:
* Fibroblast: No telomerase; telomeres shorten until senescence occurs.
* HeLa: High telomerase activity; telomere length is maintained.
* This allows cancer cells to bypass natural cell death and achieve immortality.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the template requirements of Telomerase and standard DNA Polymerase Delta.
back:
* Telomerase: Uses an internal RNA template (TERC) for synthesis.
* DNA Pol Delta: Requires an external DNA template strand.
* Both enzymes synthesize DNA in the 5' to 3' direction.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Name the specialized protein complex that binds telomeric DNA to protect chromosome ends from being recognized as double-stranded breaks.
back:
* Shelterin.
* It stabilizes the T-loop structure at chromosome ends.
* It prevents attack by nucleases and inappropriate DNA repair (NHEJ/HR).

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The noncoding hexameric repeat sequence found at the ends of human linear chromosomes is [___].
back:
● AGGGTT (base-paired with AACCCT).
● Repeated several thousand times in tandem.
● Forms a G-rich strand that is longer than the C-rich strand at the 3' end.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A researcher observes that skin fibroblasts from a patient with a premature aging syndrome (progeria) stop dividing much earlier than normal. This phenomenon is primarily due to the accelerated shortening of [___].
back:
● Telomeres.
● Reaches a critical length limit (Hayflick limit).
● Leads to cellular senescence (irreversible growth arrest).

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the TERC component within the ribonucleoprotein complex telomerase.
back:
● Acts as a short RNA template.
● Base-pairs with the single-stranded 3' end of telomeric DNA.
● Provides the sequence for TERT to synthesize new DNA repeats.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast telomere length maintenance in normal somatic cells with that in germline and malignant cells.
back:
● Somatic cells: Telomeres shorten with each division; telomerase is inactive.
● Germ/Malignant cells: Telomeres do not shorten; telomerase is active.
● Result: Somatic cells senesce; Germ/Cancer cells achieve immortality.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the biochemical limitation of DNA Polymerases that necessitates the 'end-replication' solution provided by telomerase.
back:
● Inability to initiate synthesis without a primer.
● Removal of the 5'-end RNA primer on the lagging strand leaves a gap.
● Cannot fill the extreme 5' terminal gap, causing strand shortening.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The specialized protein complex that associates with telomeric DNA to protect ends from nuclease attack and distinguish them from double-strand breaks is [___].
back:
● Shelterin.
● Stabilizes the T-loop structure.
● Prevents inappropriate DNA repair mechanisms (like nonhomologous end joining) at chromosome ends.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A biopsy of a metastatic tumor shows high expression of TERT. Describe the mechanism by which this protein facilitates the survival of neoplastic cells.
back:
● Functions as a reverse transcriptase.
● Uses an RNA template to synthesize DNA 5'→3'.
● Maintains telomere length, preventing the cell from entering senescence or apoptosis.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the specific sequence of events for extending the G-rich strand and the subsequent completion of the C-rich strand during telomere maintenance.
back:
● Telomerase extends the G-rich 3' end via reverse transcription.
● Telomerase translocates to repeat the process.
● DNA Pol-alpha (primase activity) uses the lengthened G-strand as a template to synthesize a new RNA primer/C-strand.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Differentiate between the TERT and TERC subunits regarding their biochemical nature and role in telomerase activity.
back:
● TERT: Protein component; catalytic reverse transcriptase activity.
● TERC: RNA component; serves as the template for synthesis.
● Together they form a functional ribonucleoprotein.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the biological phenomenon described as the 'mitotic clock' in aging research.
back:
● Inversely related to the number of cell divisions.
● Refers to the progressive shortening of telomeres in somatic cells.
● Predicts the remaining proliferative lifespan of a cell line.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: UV radiation typically causes the covalent joining of two adjacent pyrimidines, most commonly [___] dimers, which distort the DNA helix.
back:
• Thymine (T-T) dimers
• These intrastrand cross-links prevent replication beyond the lesion
• They are primarily repaired by Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 5-year-old child presents with extreme sensitivity to sunlight and multiple skin cancers. Analysis reveals a deficiency in the proteins required to excise pyrimidine dimers. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back:
• Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP)
• Pathophysiology: Defect in the Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) pathway
• Results in accumulation of mutations in skin cells.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the specific role of DNA Glycosylases in the Base Excision Repair (BER) mechanism.
back:
• They recognize and hydrolytically cleave abnormal bases (e.g., Uracil formed by Cytosine deamination)
• Leave an apyrimidinic or apurinic (AP) site for subsequent endonuclease action.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) with Homologous recombination (HR) regarding their accuracy and requirement for a template.
back:
• NHEJ: Error-prone and mutagenic; no template required; joins DNA fragments directly.
• HR: "Error-free"; requires homologous DNA (sister chromatid) as a template; occurs in late S/G2 phases.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the DNA repair pathway defective in Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) and name the human homologs of the bacterial Mut proteins often mutated.
back:
• Pathway: Mismatch Repair (MMR)
• Proteins: MSH2 and MLH1 (homologs of MutS and MutL)
• Leads to increased risk of colorectal and other cancers.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A point mutation that replaces a sense codon with a premature stop codon is known as a [___] mutation.
back:
• Nonsense mutation
• Results in the production of a truncated, usually nonfunctional protein
• May trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA degradation.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A patient with neurodegenerative symptoms shows an abnormally long huntingtin protein due to many extra glutamine residues. Explain the underlying genetic mutation mechanism.
back:
• Trinucleotide repeat expansion (specifically CAG repeats)
• Occurs within the coding region of the gene
• Results in toxic protein aggregates in neurons.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: In prokaryotic Mismatch Repair, how does the Mut protein system distinguish the correct parental DNA strand from the erroneous newly synthesized strand?
back:
• Based on hemimethylation
• The parental strand is methylated at GATC sequences by DNA Adenine Methylase (DAM)
• The daughter strand is temporarily unmethylated after synthesis.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between a silent mutation and a missense mutation in terms of their effect on the final polypeptide sequence.
back:
• Silent: No change in amino acid sequence due to genetic code degeneracy.
• Missense: One amino acid is replaced by another (e.g., Glutamate to Valine in Sickle Cell).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Defects in Homologous Recombination (HR) repair of double-strand breaks are primarily associated with mutations in which two high-yield genes?
back:
• BRCA1 and BRCA2
• Mutations significantly increase the risk for breast and ovarian cancers
• These genes are essential for genomic stability.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: In eukaryotic cells, the specific pathway responsible for removing bulky DNA lesions, such as pyrimidine dimers caused by UV radiation, is [___].
back:
• Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER).
• Involves endonuclease cleavage on both sides of the lesion.
• The resulting gap is filled by DNA polymerase and joined by ligase.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 35-year-old male is diagnosed with colon cancer. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the MSH2 gene, which normally coordinates the repair of replication errors. Identify the underlying repair defect.
back:
• Mismatch Repair (MMR) defect.
• Commonly involves mutations in MSH2 or MLH1.
• Clinically manifests as Lynch Syndrome (Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the initial enzymatic step in Base Excision Repair (BER) when a cytosine undergoes spontaneous deamination to uracil.
back:
• DNA Glycosylase recognizes and removes the abnormal uracil base.
• It cleaves the N-glycosidic bond, leaving an apyrimidinic (AP) site.
• AP-endonuclease then nicks the phosphodiester backbone to initiate repair.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast the fidelity and timing of Non-homologous End Joining (NHEJ) with Homologous Recombination (HR) in repairing double-strand breaks.
back:
• NHEJ: Error-prone (mutagenic), may lose DNA; occurs throughout the cell cycle.
• HR: High-fidelity (error-free), uses sister chromatid template; occurs in late S/G2 phases.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the functional consequence of a nonsense mutation occurring within the coding region of a tumor suppressor gene.
back:
• Creates a premature termination (stop) codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA).
• Results in a truncated, usually non-functional protein.
• Leads to loss of tumor suppression, promoting oncogenesis.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A child presenting with extreme photosensitivity, multiple skin carcinomas at a young age, and defective pyrimidine dimer removal likely suffers from [___].
back:
• Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP).
• Caused by autosomal recessive mutations in Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) genes.
• Leads to massive accumulation of UV-induced DNA damage.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A woman with a strong family history of early-onset breast and ovarian cancer is found to have a BRCA1 mutation. Specify the DNA repair process that is impaired in this patient.
back:
• Homologous Recombination (HR).
• BRCA1 and BRCA2 proteins are essential for error-free repair of double-strand breaks.
• Loss leads to genomic instability and high cancer risk.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: How does trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene lead to the pathophysiology of Huntington disease?
back:
• CAG repeats expand in exon 1, adding extra glutamine residues.
• Produces an abnormally long protein that is cleaved into toxic fragments.
• Fragments aggregate in neurons, causing progressive neurodegeneration.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between a silent mutation and a missense mutation regarding their effect on the final polypeptide sequence.
back:
• Silent: Base change codes for the same amino acid; no change in protein structure.
• Missense: Base change codes for a different amino acid; alters primary protein sequence.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the specific base formed when cytosine undergoes spontaneous deamination, and name the repair pathway that corrects it.
back:
• Uracil is formed from cytosine deamination.
• This is corrected by the Base Excision Repair (BER) pathway.
• Prevents GC to AT transition mutations in the genome.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The tandemly repeated hexameric sequence that characterizes the ends of human linear chromosomes is [___].
back:
• AGGGTT (base-paired to AACCCT)
• Found in several thousand repeats
• Forms the structural basis of telomeres

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A biopsy of a metastatic osteosarcoma reveals cells that avoid the 'mitotic clock' and divide indefinitely. This immortality is primarily achieved by the upregulation of [___].
back:
• Telomerase
• Prevents replicative senescence
• Maintains telomere length in 90% of cancers

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the biochemical role of the TERC (RNA) component within the telomerase ribonucleoprotein complex.
back:
• Acts as an internal template
• Provides the sequence for DNA synthesis
• Base-pairs with the G-rich 3' overhang

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Contrast the 'end-replication problem' in somatic cells versus germline cells.
back:
• Somatic: Lack telomerase; telomeres shorten until senescence occurs.
• Germline: Express active telomerase; telomere length is preserved for offspring.

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Identify the specific enzymatic activity of the TERT protein subunit of telomerase.
back:
• Reverse transcriptase activity
• RNA-directed DNA polymerase
• Extends the 3' end of the G-rich strand

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The specialized protein complex that sequester the 3' single-stranded overhang to prevent DNA repair machinery from recognizing it as a double-strand break is [___].
back:
• Shelterin
• Maintains structural integrity
• Protects against nuclease attack

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of Telomeres in Aging
front: A child presents with skin wrinkling and alopecia, diagnosed with a progeria. The underlying molecular pathophysiology involves accelerated [___].
back:
• Telomere shortening (attrition)
• Leads to premature cellular senescence
• Impairs tissue regeneration and repair

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the requirement for DNA Polymerase Alpha in telomere lengthening after telomerase has extended the 3' overhang.
back:
• Provides primase activity
• Synthesizes an RNA primer on the new G-rich template
• Allows completion of the complementary C-rich strand

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between the B-form DNA of the chromosome body and the structure of the extreme 3' telomeric end.
back:
• Chromosome body: Double-stranded B-DNA
• Telomeric end: Single-stranded G-rich overhang
• Overhang often folds into a protective loop

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Name the phase of the cell cycle during which telomerase typically performs the extension of chromosome ends.
back:
• S-phase (Synthesis phase)
• Occurs concurrently with genomic DNA replication

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: In humans, telomeric DNA consists of several thousand tandem repeats of the noncoding hexameric sequence [___].
back: - AGGGTT - This sequence is found on the G-rich strand of linear chromosomes - It base-pairs with a complementary AACCCT sequence - These repeats maintain the structural integrity and stability of chromosomal ends

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A laboratory study observes that most normal human somatic cells stop dividing after a specific number of cycles. This phenomenon, known as senescence, is primarily caused by [___].
back: - Telomere shortening - Somatic cells lack telomerase and cannot replicate the extreme 5' end of the lagging strand - Shortening beyond a critical length triggers the mitotic clock, leading to cellular senescence or apoptosis

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the role of the telomerase RNA component (TERC) by contrasting its function with that of a typical DNA primase.
back: - TERC: Acts as an internal, permanent RNA template for reverse transcription at chromosomal ends - DNA Primase: Synthesizes transient, short RNA primers to provide the 3'-OH group required for standard DNA polymerase activity

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
coreConcept: Telomerase in Somatic vs Cancer Cells
front: Contrast the proliferative capacity of a patient's normal skin fibroblasts with their malignant melanoma cells in the context of telomerase expression.
back: - Skin Fibroblasts: Telomerase is inactive; telomeres shorten with every division until reaching senescence - Malignant Melanoma: Telomerase is constitutively active; telomere length is maintained, allowing the cells to bypass the mitotic clock and achieve immortality

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Describe the specific enzymatic activity of TERT, which is currently a primary target for experimental anti-cancer pharmacological inhibitors.
back: - RNA-directed DNA polymerase (Reverse Transcriptase) - It uses an internal RNA template to extend the 3' G-rich telomeric strand - Inhibition prevents cancer cells from maintaining telomere length, eventually inducing senescence or cell death

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: The specialized protein complex required to protect chromosomal ends and prevent their recognition as damaged DNA is [___].
back: - Shelterin - It coats telomeric DNA and stabilizes the terminal loop structure - Deficiency or mutation in shelterin proteins is clinically associated with bone marrow failure and certain premature aging syndromes

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: A 5-year-old child presents with signs of premature aging, including grey hair and thin skin. Biopsy suggests a defect in the TERT gene. This clinical presentation is best explained by [___].
back: - Accelerated telomere shortening - Deficiency in telomerase leads to premature cellular senescence - This results in early depletion of stem cell pools and the loss of tissue regenerative capacity, causing a progeroid appearance

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Explain the mechanism behind the 'end-replication problem' by contrasting the synthesis of the 3' end of the leading strand versus the 5' end of the lagging strand.
back: - Leading Strand: Synthesized continuously to the very tip of the chromosome - Lagging Strand: Removal of the terminal RNA primer leaves a gap that DNA polymerase cannot fill due to the lack of a 3'-OH upstream

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: Distinguish between TERT and TERC in the physiological cycle of telomere extension.
back: - TERT: The catalytic protein subunit that functions as a reverse transcriptase - TERC: The essential RNA subunit that provides the specific hexameric template - Together they form the ribonucleoprotein complex that prevents genomic shortening during replication

category: Discuss telomeres and Telomerase and their clinical significance
front: List the two primary non-malignant cell types in the human body that express high levels of telomerase to maintain chromosomal length.
back: - Germ cells (gametes) and stem cells - These cells maintain telomerase activity to prevent chromosome shortening across generations - This ensures genomic stability and allows for continuous tissue renewal and gametogenesis

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: In Base Excision Repair, the specific enzyme that hydrolytically cleaves an abnormal base from the deoxyribose-phosphate backbone is [___].
back:
• DNA Glycosylase
• Recognizes specific lesions like uracil or oxidized bases
• Cleaves the N-glycosidic bond
• Creates an apyrimidinic or apurinic (AP) site

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 6-year-old child presents with extreme sensitivity to sunlight and multiple facial carcinomas. This condition likely results from a defect in [___].
back:
• Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)
• Failure to excise UV-induced pyrimidine (thymine) dimers
• Caused by mutations in XP proteins (uvrABC exinucleases)
• Leads to Xeroderma Pigmentosum

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain how prokaryotic cells identify the correct template strand for repair during methyl-directed mismatch repair.
back:
• Relies on hemimethylation status at GATC sequences
• Parental strands are methylated by DAM methylase
• Newly synthesized strands are temporarily unmethylated
• Mut proteins specifically nick the unmethylated daughter strand

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast Nonhomologous End Joining (NHEJ) with Homologous Recombination (HR) regarding their fidelity in repairing double-strand breaks.
back:
• NHEJ: Error-prone and mutagenic; ligates broken ends without a template; loses DNA sequence.
• HR: Error-free; uses a homologous sister chromatid as a template; occurs during late S/G2 phases.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the molecular consequence of CAG triplet expansion in the huntingtin gene coding region.
back:
• Insertion of extra Glutamine residues (Polyglutamine)
• Produces an abnormally long, misfolded protein
• Toxic fragments aggregate in neurons
• Leads to Huntington disease neurodegeneration

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) is caused by inherited mutations in the proteins involved in [___].
back:
• Mismatch Repair (MMR)
• Specifically MSH2 or MLH1 (human Mut homologs)
• Increases risk for early-onset colon and ovarian cancers
• Allows replication errors to persist as mutations

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A spontaneous deamination converts Cytosine into Uracil in DNA. Identify the repair pathway triggered and the first enzyme involved.
back:
• Pathway: Base Excision Repair (BER)
• Enzyme: Uracil-DNA Glycosylase
• Removes the deaminated base to prevent point mutations
• Resulting AP site is subsequently repaired by endonucleases

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Detail the roles of AP endonuclease and deoxyribose phosphate lyase in the repair of abasic sites.
back:
• AP Endonuclease: Recognizes missing bases and nicks the 5' side of the AP site.
• Lyase: Removes the single, base-free sugar-phosphate residue.
• Provides a 3'-OH for DNA Polymerase I

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between a missense mutation and a nonsense mutation regarding their effect on the final protein product.
back:
• Missense: Single nucleotide change results in a different amino acid insertion.
• Nonsense: Single nucleotide change creates a premature stop codon, causing protein truncation.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the DNA repair pathway associated with BRCA1/BRCA2 and the primary clinical risks of its deficiency.
back:
• Pathway: Homologous Recombination (HR)
• Function: Error-free repair of double-strand DNA breaks
• Clinical Risks: Significantly increased risk for breast and ovarian cancers

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: The specific DNA repair pathway responsible for removing bulky lesions such as pyrimidine dimers caused by UV radiation is [___].
back: - Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) - Employs uvrABC excinuclease in prokaryotes - Pathway is defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 5-year-old child presents with extreme sun sensitivity, severe freckling, and early onset of skin carcinoma. Identify the underlying diagnostic defect.
back: - Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) - Defective Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) - Inability to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the specific role of DNA glycosylases in the Base Excision Repair (BER) pathway.
back: - Hydrolytically cleaves abnormal/damaged bases from the sugar-phosphate backbone - Creates an apurinic or apyrimidinic (AP) site - Recognizes specific lesions like uracil in DNA

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) and Homologous Recombination (HR) regarding accuracy and cell cycle timing.
back: - NHEJ: Error-prone and mutagenic; occurs throughout the cell cycle - HR: High-fidelity (error-free); limited to late S and G2 phases - HR requires a homologous template

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the clinical condition and molecular defect associated with mutations in the MSH2 or MLH1 genes.
back: - Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC) - Defective Mismatch Repair (MMR) - Leads to microsatellite instability and increased colorectal cancer risk

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A point mutation that replaces a sense codon with a termination codon, leading to a truncated protein product, is a [___] mutation.
back: - Nonsense mutation - Results in premature termination of translation - Often leads to nonfunctional protein degradation

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A patient is diagnosed with Sickle Cell Anemia due to a GAG to GTG substitution at codon 6. Classify this mutation and the resulting amino acid change.
back: - Missense mutation - Glutamate is replaced by Valine - Results in altered hemoglobin solubility and cell sickling

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain how the E. coli repair machinery distinguishes between the correct parental strand and the erroneous daughter strand during Mismatch Repair (MMR).
back: - Based on hemimethylation status - Parental strand is methylated at GATC by DAM methylase - Unmethylated daughter strand is identified as the target for repair

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between silent and missense mutations regarding their effect on the resulting polypeptide.
back: - Silent: No change in amino acid sequence due to code degeneracy - Missense: Replacement of one amino acid with a different one - Both are types of point mutations

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Name the specific enzyme that recognizes the lack of a base (AP site) and initiates repair by cleaving the DNA backbone.
back: - AP-endonuclease - Cleaves the 5' side of the sugar-phosphate residue - Part of the Base Excision Repair (BER) mechanism

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
coreConcept: Xeroderma Pigmentosum and Nucleotide Excision Repair
front: In the autosomal recessive disorder [___], a deficiency in nucleotide excision repair proteins leads to an inability to remove pyrimidine dimers caused by ultraviolet radiation.
back: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP). * Results in extreme sensitivity to sunlight. * Leads to early and frequent development of multiple skin cancers.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 45-year-old male is diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Genetic testing reveals mutations in the MSH2 and MLH1 genes. Identify the most likely clinical syndrome and the specific DNA repair pathway affected.
back: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC). * Defect in Mismatch Repair (MMR). * MSH2 and MLH1 are human homologs of bacterial Mut proteins.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the role of DNA glycosylases and AP endonucleases in the Base Excision Repair (BER) of a deaminated cytosine.
back: * DNA glycosylase removes the abnormal uracil, creating an AP site. * AP endonuclease nicks the 5' side of the AP site. * Deoxyribose phosphate lyase removes the sugar-phosphate residue before gap filling.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast Nonhomologous End Joining (NHEJ) with Homologous Recombination (HR) regarding their accuracy and requirement for a DNA template.
back: * NHEJ: Error-prone; no template used; ligates two DNA ends. * HR: Error-free (accurate); uses sister chromatid/homologous DNA as template; occurs in late S/G2 phases.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: The neurodegenerative disorder Huntington disease is caused by the [___] of CAG triplets within the coding region of the huntingtin gene.
back: Trinucleotide repeat expansion. * Results in polyglutamine tracts in the huntingtin protein. * Leads to toxic protein fragments that aggregate in neurons.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the type of mutation where a single nucleotide change results in the creation of a UAA, UAG, or UGA codon.
back: Nonsense mutation. * Results in premature termination of translation. * Produces a truncated protein that is often nonfunctional or degraded.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A patient with anemia is found to have a GAG to GTG mutation at codon 6 of the beta-globin gene. Identify the mutation type and the resulting amino acid substitution.
back: Missense mutation. * Glutamate is replaced by Valine. * Results in Hemoglobin S (HbS) which polymerizes under low oxygen conditions.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the mechanism of 'strand discrimination' in prokaryotic mismatch repair involving the DAM methylase.
back: * GATC sequences are methylated on the parental strand by DAM methylase. * The newly synthesized daughter strand is transiently unmethylated. * Mut proteins identify and repair the unmethylated strand.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between a silent mutation and a missense mutation regarding the primary structure of the encoded protein.
back: * Silent: Codon change specifies the same amino acid; no change in protein sequence. * Missense: Codon change specifies a different amino acid; alters the polypeptide chain.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes increase the risk of breast and ovarian cancer due to defects in [___].
back: Homologous Recombination (HR). * This 'error-free' system repairs double-strand DNA breaks. * Loss of repair leads to genomic instability and oncogenesis.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: The rare genetic disorder characterized by an inability to repair pyrimidine dimers caused by UV light is [___].
back: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP). - Caused by defects in Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) proteins. - Results in extensive skin mutations and multiple early-onset skin cancers.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 45-year-old patient with a history of colon cancer presents with a new tumor showing microsatellite instability. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in MSH2 or MLH1. Identify the condition and the defective repair pathway.
back: Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC). - Defective DNA Mismatch Repair (MMR). - Mutations in human homologs of bacterial Mut proteins lead to increased colorectal and other cancer risks.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the specific role of DNA Glycosylases within the Base Excision Repair (BER) mechanism.
back: They recognize and hydrolytically cleave abnormal bases (like uracil from cytosine deamination). - This action leaves behind an apyrimidinic or apurinic (AP) site for further processing.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast Nonhomologous End Joining (NHEJ) with Homologous Recombination (HR) regarding their template requirements and error potential.
back: NHEJ: No template used; error-prone and mutagenic; can occur throughout the cell cycle. - HR: Uses homologous DNA as a template; high-fidelity ('error-free'); limited to late S and G2 phases.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain how a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the coding region affects protein structure in Huntington disease.
back: It inserts multiple extra glutamine residues (polyglutamine tail). - This creates an abnormally long protein that is cleaved into toxic fragments which aggregate in neurons.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A mutation that converts a sense codon into a termination codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) is called a [___] mutation.
back: Nonsense mutation. - Results in a truncated (shortened) protein product. - Often leads to nonfunctional proteins or nonsense-mediated mRNA degradation.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A child presents with painful crises and hemolytic anemia. Sequencing reveals a GAG to GTG point mutation in the beta-globin gene. Identify the type of mutation and the resulting amino acid change.
back: Missense mutation. - Glutamate is replaced by Valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain. - Produces Hemoglobin S (HbS).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the mechanism of strand discrimination used during Mismatch Repair (MMR) in prokaryotes.
back: Utilizes hemimethylation. - Parental strands are methylated at GATC sequences by DAM methylase. - The unmethylated (newly synthesized) strand is identified and repaired.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish the types of DNA damage addressed by Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) versus Base Excision Repair (BER).
back: NER: Handles bulky, helix-distorting lesions (e.g., pyrimidine dimers, benzo[a]pyrene adducts). - BER: Handles single-base alterations (e.g., uracil, alkylated bases, or spontaneous base loss).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the enzyme that recognizes a missing base and makes an endonucleolytic cut at the AP site during DNA repair.
back: AP Endonuclease. - It nicks the phosphodiester backbone on the 5' side of the apurinic or apyrimidinic site to initiate gap filling.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: In the Base Excision Repair (BER) pathway, the specific enzyme that recognizes and hydrolytically removes an abnormal base from the deoxyribose-phosphate backbone is [___].
back: DNA glycosylase.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 45-year-old male with a significant family history of early-onset colorectal cancer is diagnosed with Lynch Syndrome. Identify the specific DNA repair pathway that is defective in this patient.
back:
* Mismatch Repair (MMR).
* Pathophysiology: Mutations in proteins like MSH2 or MLH1 prevent the correction of replication errors that escape proofreading.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the multi-step mechanism by which human skin cells correct bulky lesions, such as thymine dimers, caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
back:
* Recognition: Specific endonucleases (excinucleases) identify the dimer.
* Excision: The damaged strand is cleaved on both sides of the lesion.
* Gap Filling: DNA polymerase I (prokaryotes) or delta/epsilon (eukaryotes) fills the gap.
* Ligation: DNA ligase seals the nick.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between Nonhomologous End Joining (NHEJ) and Homologous Recombination (HR) regarding their fidelity and dependency on the cell cycle.
back:
* NHEJ: Error-prone, involves direct ligation of ends, occurs anytime (predominantly G1).
* HR: Error-free, requires a homologous sister chromatid as a template, occurs in late S or G2 phases.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the pharmacological target of the chemotherapeutic agent etoposide during the process of DNA replication and repair.
back: Human Type II Topoisomerase.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Mutations in the [___] genes account for the majority of cases of Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC) by compromising the fidelity of DNA replication.
back: MSH2 and MLH1.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: An 8-year-old child presents with extreme sensitivity to sunlight and multiple basal cell carcinomas. Molecular studies suggest a failure to repair pyrimidine dimers. State the likely diagnosis and the specific defective repair process.
back:
* Diagnosis: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP).
* Defect: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER), often due to deficiencies in XP proteins (e.g., UV-specific endonuclease).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the biological mechanism used by the bacterial Mismatch Repair (MMR) system to distinguish the parental DNA template from the newly synthesized daughter strand containing an error.
back:
* Parent strand: Methylated at GATC sequences by DAM methylase.
* Daughter strand: Temporarily hemimethylated (unmethylated) immediately following replication.
* Recognition: Mut proteins identify the mismatch on the unmethylated strand.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast the resulting protein products of a missense mutation versus a nonsense mutation in a coding sequence.
back:
* Missense: A single nucleotide change results in one different amino acid in the polypeptide.
* Nonsense: A single nucleotide change creates a premature stop codon, leading to a truncated protein.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the specific enzyme that recognizes an apyrimidinic or apurinic (AP) site and initiates repair by cleaving the 5′ side of the sugar-phosphate backbone.
back: AP endonuclease.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: The specific DNA repair pathway responsible for identifying and removing bulky pyrimidine dimers caused by exposure to ultraviolet radiation is [___].
back:
*   Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER).
*   Utilizes uvrABC excinuclease in bacteria.
*   Defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum.
*   Cleaves the phosphodiester backbone on both sides of the lesion.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 45-year-old male presents with colorectal cancer. Genetic analysis identifies a mutation in the MSH2 gene, affecting the proteins that coordinate mismatch repair. Identify the likely clinical diagnosis.
back:
*   Lynch Syndrome (Hereditary Nonpolyposis Colorectal Cancer/HNPCC).
*   Caused by defective mismatch repair (MMR).
*   Increases risk for colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.
*   Involves mutations in human homologs of bacterial Mut proteins.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the precise role of DNA glycosylases within the Base Excision Repair (BER) mechanism.
back:
*   Recognize specific abnormal or chemically modified bases (e.g., uracil).
*   Hydrolytically cleave the N-glycosidic bond between the base and sugar.
*   Leaves behind an apurinic or apyrimidinic (AP) site for further processing.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast the functional outcomes and fidelity of Non-homologous End Joining (NHEJ) with Homologous Recombination (HR) in repairing double-strand breaks.
back:
*   NHEJ: Directly ligates broken ends; occurs anytime; error-prone; results in DNA loss.
*   HR: Uses sister chromatid as a template; occurs in S/G2 phases; error-free (high fidelity).
*   HR involves BRCA1/2 proteins.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the molecular effect of a nonsense mutation on the translation of a protein-coding sequence.
back:
*   Converts a sense codon into a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA).
*   Triggers premature termination of polypeptide chain synthesis.
*   Produces a truncated protein that is typically non-functional and rapidly degraded.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Following the removal of an abnormal base by a glycosylase, the enzyme [___] is required to initiate the next step of the repair by nicking the 5' side of the AP site.
back:
*   AP endonuclease.
*   Recognizes missing bases in the DNA backbone.
*   Works in tandem with deoxyribose phosphate lyase to remove the sugar-phosphate residue.
*   Prepares the gap for DNA Polymerase I.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 32-year-old female with a strong family history of breast cancer is found to have a mutation in the BRCA1 gene. Explain the specific DNA repair deficiency associated with this finding.
back:
*   Defect in Homologous Recombination (HR).
*   Inability to repair double-strand breaks with high fidelity.
*   Leads to genomic instability and significantly increased risk for breast and ovarian malignancies.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the mechanism by which Escherichia coli discriminates between the template and the newly synthesized strand during mismatch repair (MMR).
back:
*   Based on the degree of methylation at GATC sequences.
*   The parental strand is methylated by DAM methylase.
*   The daughter strand is transiently unmethylated (hemimethylated) after replication, marking it for excision.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between a silent mutation and a missense mutation regarding their impact on the protein's primary structure.
back:
*   Silent: Nucleotide change codes for the same amino acid; no effect on protein structure.
*   Missense: Nucleotide change results in a different amino acid; may alter protein function (e.g., HbS).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain why the addition or deletion of two nucleotides in a coding sequence is more deleterious than the addition of three nucleotides.
back:
*   Two-base change: Causes a frameshift mutation; alters the entire downstream reading frame.
*   Three-base change: Adds/removes a single amino acid (in-frame); preserves the downstream sequence (e.g., ΔF508 in Cystic Fibrosis).

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: In the context of DNA repair, Xeroderma pigmentosum is primarily caused by an inherited deficiency in the [___] pathway.
back: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER). This pathway specifically removes bulky DNA lesions and pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A 5-year-old child presents with extreme photosensitivity, severe skin blistering after minimal sun exposure, and numerous freckle-like lentigines. Biopsy of a suspicious lesion confirms squamous cell carcinoma. State the likely diagnosis.
back: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP). It presents early in life with marked cutaneous sensitivity and a vastly increased risk of skin malignancies.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Explain the biochemical consequence of the specific DNA repair failure that occurs in Xeroderma pigmentosum upon exposure to ultraviolet light.
back: Failure to excise pyrimidine dimers (thymine dimers). This results in the accumulation of bulky DNA adducts that distort the double helix.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Contrast the genetic defect in Xeroderma pigmentosum with the molecular pathology of Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC) regarding the type of DNA repair involved.
back: XP involves a defect in Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) for bulky lesions, while Lynch Syndrome involves a defect in Mismatch Repair (MMR) for replication errors.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Identify the specific enzyme activity that is typically absent or non-functional at the site of a thymine dimer in an XP patient's skin cells.
back: UV-specific endonuclease (excinuclease). This enzyme is required to nick the DNA strand on both sides of the bulky dimer to initiate removal.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: In a patient with Xeroderma pigmentosum, the inheritance pattern of the disease is strictly [___].
back: Autosomal recessive. The condition requires two defective copies of one of the seven identified XP genes (XPA-XPG).

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A laboratory report indicates that a patient's fibroblasts show high rates of chromosomal mutations following low-dose UV radiation compared to healthy controls. Relate this finding to the pathogenesis of early-onset skin cancer.
back: Unrepaired pyrimidine dimers lead to translesion synthesis errors. These permanent mutations accumulate in oncogenes and tumor suppressors, driving carcinogenesis.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Describe why patients with Xeroderma pigmentosum must avoid even indirect sunlight and fluorescent lighting in severe cases.
back: The DNA damage (pyrimidine dimers) is cumulative. Without a functional NER system, every exposure increases the mutational burden and risk of malignancy.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Differentiate between the structural DNA changes addressed by Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) in XP and those handled by Base Excision Repair (BER).
back: NER handles bulky, helix-distorting lesions (e.g., UV dimers); BER handles non-bulky, single-base damage (e.g., deaminated bases like uracil).

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Which group of seven genes is responsible for the majority of clinical complementation groups observed in Xeroderma pigmentosum?
back: XP genes (XPA through XPG). These encode the various proteins of the multi-subunit NER complex.

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: The creation of an 'AP site' (apurinic or apyrimidinic) occurs during the [___] pathway after a specific enzyme removes a damaged or abnormal nitrogenous base.
back:
• Base Excision Repair (BER)
• Involves DNA glycosylases
• Cleaves the N-glycosidic bond
• Leaves the sugar-phosphate backbone intact initially

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 40-year-old patient with a strong family history of nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) is found to have a mutation in the MSH2 gene. Identify the defective DNA repair pathway.
back:
• Mismatch Repair (MMR)
• Corrects errors escaping proofreading
• Defects increase risk for colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers
• Mediated by human homologs of bacterial Mut proteins

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the biochemical basis of strand discrimination used by E. coli to ensure the correct strand is fixed during mismatch repair.
back:
• DNA adenine methylase (DAM) methylates GATC sequences
• Parental strands are methylated; new daughter strands are temporarily unmethylated
• Mut proteins target the unmethylated (incorrect) strand for repair

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast the biological accuracy and template requirements of Non-homologous End Joining (NHEJ) versus Homologous Recombination (HR) in repairing double-strand breaks.
back:
• NHEJ: No template required; error-prone/mutagenic; occurs throughout cell cycle
• HR: Requires homologous DNA template (sister chromatid); error-free; occurs in late S/G2 phases

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe the pharmacological mechanism by which the chemotherapeutic agent Doxorubicin induces cytotoxic effects in cancer cells.
back:
• Induces double-strand breaks in DNA
• Generates oxidative free radicals
• Overwhelms DNA repair capacity
• Triggers apoptosis in rapidly dividing cells

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: The clinical presentation of extreme sun sensitivity and multiple early-onset skin cancers in Xeroderma Pigmentosum is caused by a failure in [___].
back:
• Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)
• Inability to repair pyrimidine (thymine) dimers
• Deficiency in XP proteins/UV-specific endonucleases
• Accumulation of sunlight-induced mutations

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A genetic study of a patient with cystic fibrosis reveals a three-base deletion (ΔF508) in the CFTR gene. Explain why this mutation is described as an 'in-frame' deletion.
back:
• Removes one entire codon (Phenylalanine)
• Does not shift the reading frame of subsequent codons
• Results in a misfolded protein rather than a truncated sequence

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Detail the sequential enzymatic steps required for Base Excision Repair (BER) once a damaged base is recognized.
back:
• DNA glycosylase removes base (AP site)
• AP-endonuclease nicks 5' side of lesion
• Deoxyribose phosphate lyase removes sugar-phosphate residue
• DNA Polymerase and Ligase fill and seal gap

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between the identification of the 'mismatched' strand in prokaryotes versus eukaryotes.
back:
• Prokaryotes: Use hemimethylation status at GATC sites
• Eukaryotes: Likely recognize nicks/discontinuities in the nascent strand
• Both: Discriminate between parental and daughter strands to preserve genomic integrity

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the primary DNA lesion caused by non-ionizing ultraviolet (UV) radiation and specify the bonds involved.
back:
• Pyrimidine dimers (typically Thymine-Thymine)
• Covalent joining of two adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand
• Creates bulky intrastrand cross-links that block DNA polymerase

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare genetic condition characterized by a deficiency in the [___] pathway, which is responsible for fixing UV-induced DNA damage.
back: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: An 8-year-old child presents with extreme sensitivity to sunlight and numerous freckles on the face and neck. A biopsy of a suspicious lesion reveals basal cell carcinoma. Identify the most likely underlying molecular defect.
back: Defective Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) preventing the removal of pyrimidine dimers.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Explain the biochemical consequence of ultraviolet (UV) radiation on the DNA of a patient with Xeroderma pigmentosum.
back: UV radiation causes intrastrand pyrimidine dimers (thymine-thymine). In XP, these lesions cannot be excised, leading to an accumulation of DNA mutations and subsequent carcinogenesis.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A patient with skin lesions is suspected of having either Lynch syndrome or Xeroderma pigmentosum. Contrast the specific DNA repair systems affected in these two conditions.
back: Lynch syndrome involves Mismatch Repair (MMR) defects. Xeroderma pigmentosum involves Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) defects.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Identify the specific type of DNA lesion that typically accumulates in the skin cells of a patient suffering from Xeroderma pigmentosum.
back: Bulky, helix-distorting pyrimidine dimers (covalent joining of adjacent pyrimidines, usually thymines) caused by UV radiation.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: In Xeroderma pigmentosum, the inability to repair pyrimidine dimers results in an extensive accumulation of [___], leading to numerous skin cancers at a young age.
back: DNA mutations

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A pediatrician notes that a 5-year-old patient has developed multiple skin cancers despite limited outdoor activity. Genetic testing confirms an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Name this condition.
back: Xeroderma pigmentosum

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Describe the specific role of the seven distinct 'XP proteins' in the maintenance of genomic integrity in human skin cells.
back: These proteins participate in global genomic and transcription-coupled repair by recognizing bulky lesions, cleaving the damaged strand, and allowing excision.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Distinguish between the types of DNA damage repaired by Base Excision Repair (BER) versus the system deficient in Xeroderma pigmentosum.
back: BER removes small, non-bulky base alterations (e.g., deaminated cytosine). The system in XP (NER) removes bulky, helix-distorting lesions (e.g., pyrimidine dimers).

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: State the inheritance pattern and the primary environmental trigger for the clinical manifestations of Xeroderma pigmentosum.
back: Inheritance: Autosomal recessive. Trigger: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation (Sunlight).

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: In humans, the specific excision repair pathway responsible for identifying and removing bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as pyrimidine dimers is [___].
back:
* Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)
* Utilizes specific excinucleases to cleave the damaged strand
* Fills gaps using DNA Polymerase and Ligase
* Crucial for preventing UV-induced skin malignancies

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A 5-year-old child presents with severe photosensitivity, excessive facial freckling, and several early-onset basal cell carcinomas. Identify the most likely genetic diagnosis and the underlying molecular failure.
back:
* Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP)
* Defective Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) proteins
* Inability to excise thymine dimers caused by UV light
* Leads to rapid accumulation of oncogenic mutations

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism used by the cell to correct the spontaneous deamination of cytosine to uracil in the DNA backbone.
back:
* Base Excision Repair (BER)
* Uracil-DNA glycosylase removes the abnormal base
* AP-endonuclease nicks the sugar-phosphate backbone
* DNA Polymerase I and Ligase complete the repair

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Contrast the repair of double-strand DNA breaks via Non-homologous End Joining (NHEJ) and Homologous Recombination (HR) regarding their accuracy.
back:
* NHEJ: Error-prone and mutagenic; joins ends without a template
* HR: High-fidelity and error-free; uses homologous DNA as a template
* NHEJ occurs throughout the cell cycle; HR in S/G2 phases

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Describe how the prokaryotic methyl-directed mismatch repair system distinguishes the correct parental strand from the mutated daughter strand.
back:
* GATC sequences are methylated by DNA Adenine Methylase (DAM)
* New daughter strands are temporarily hemimethylated (unmethylated)
* Mut proteins recognize mismatches on the unmethylated strand
* Ensures repair uses the accurate parental template

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) is characterized by inherited mutations in human homologs of bacterial [___] proteins.
back:
* Mut proteins (specifically MSH2 or MLH1)
* Results in defective Mismatch Repair (MMR)
* Leads to microsatellite instability in the genome
* Significantly increases risk for colon and endometrial cancers

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: A patient presents with choreiform movements and progressive dementia; genetic analysis reveals a CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene. Identify the mutation type and the consequence on the protein product.
back:
* Trinucleotide repeat expansion
* Insertion of excessive glutamine residues (polyglutamine tract)
* Produces an abnormally long, toxic protein
* Protein fragments aggregate, leading to neuronal death

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Explain why a single nucleotide deletion often results in a nonfunctional, truncated protein even if the deletion occurs far from the original stop codon.
back:
* Causes a Frameshift Mutation, altering the reading frame
* Changes all subsequent amino acids in the sequence
* Likely creates a premature nonsense (stop) codon downstream
* Results in premature translation termination and a shortened peptide

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Distinguish between Silent and Missense point mutations in terms of their impact on the final amino acid sequence.
back:
* Silent: Base change results in the same amino acid (degeneracy)
* Missense: Base change results in a different amino acid
* Silent has no phenotypic effect; Missense may alter protein function

category: Describe DNA repair, mutation and cancers
front: Identify the primary molecular lesion induced by ultraviolet (UV) radiation and its immediate effect on DNA replication.
back:
* Formation of intrastrand pyrimidine (thymine) dimers
* Covalent joining of adjacent bases distorts the double helix
* Blocks the progress of DNA Polymerase during synthesis
* High risk of permanent mutation if not repaired by NER

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare genetic disorder characterized by a deficiency in the [___] pathway.
back:
• Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER)
• Pathway repairs bulky DNA lesions like pyrimidine dimers
• Damage is typically caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A 5-year-old child presents with extreme photosensitivity and extensive freckling on the face and neck. Biopsy of a suspicious lesion reveals a basal cell carcinoma. The most likely molecular defect involves [___].
back:
• Inability to repair UV-induced DNA damage
• Deficiency in UV-specific endonuclease (excinuclease)
• Intrastrand cross-links (pyrimidine dimers) accumulate in the genome

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Explain the biochemical consequence of ultraviolet (UV) light exposure on the DNA of a patient lacking functional XP proteins.
back:
• Formation of covalent bonds between adjacent pyrimidines (thymine dimers)
• Failure of the uvrABC/NER complex to excise the lesion
• Accumulation of mutations leads to early oncogenic transformation

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Contrast the DNA repair defect in Xeroderma Pigmentosum with that of Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC).
back:
• XP: Defective NER; cannot repair UV-induced bulky lesions.
• Lynch: Defective Mismatch Repair (MMR); cannot fix replication errors.
• XP presents with skin cancers; Lynch with colorectal/endometrial cancers.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Identify the mode of inheritance for Xeroderma Pigmentosum and the general function of the mutated gene products.
back:
• Autosomal recessive inheritance
• Gene products (XPA–XPG) function as endonucleases and helicases
• Essential for identifying and removing damaged DNA segments

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: In Xeroderma Pigmentosum, the enzyme [___] fails to recognize and cleave the damaged DNA strand on both sides of a bulky pyrimidine dimer.
back:
• UV-specific endonuclease (uvrABC excinuclease equivalent)
• Performs the 'incision' step in excision repair
• Leaves a gap for DNA Polymerase I/epsilon and Ligase

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A patient's fibroblast culture shows a 90% reduction in DNA repair synthesis following UV irradiation. Correlate this laboratory data with the patient's clinical risk profile.
back:
• Confirms a profound defect in the NER system
• High susceptibility to sunlight-induced mutations in tumor suppressors
• 1000-fold increased risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Describe the sequential steps of DNA repair that are compromised specifically when the damage-recognition protein XPA is mutated.
back:
• Damage recognition: Failure to detect helix-distorting dimers
• Excision: Subsequent recruitment of TFIIH and endonucleases is blocked
• Result: Persistent DNA lesions stall transcription and replication

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Distinguish between the types of DNA damage targeted by Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) versus Base Excision Repair (BER).
back:
• NER (XP): Bulky, helix-distorting lesions (e.g., thymine dimers)
• BER: Non-bulky damage (e.g., deaminated cytosine to uracil)
• XP specifically affects the repair of large chemical adducts and dimers

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: List the three cardinal clinical features required to diagnose Xeroderma Pigmentosum on a UHS Board exam.
back:
• Severe photosensitivity (sunburn with minimal UV exposure)
• Early-onset, extensive lentigines (freckle-like pigmentation)
• Multiple cutaneous malignancies (BCC, SCC, Melanoma) in childhood

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Xeroderma pigmentosum is characterized by an autosomal recessive deficiency in the [___] repair pathway.
back: * Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER). * Specifically involves a lack of UV-specific endonuclease activity.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A 4-year-old child presents with severe photosensitivity, extensive lentigines, and a recently diagnosed skin malignancy. Identify the underlying biochemical defect.
back: * Defective excision of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. * Accumulation of DNA mutations due to unrepaired sunlight-induced damage.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Explain the specific action of the enzyme that is typically deficient in patients with Xeroderma pigmentosum.
back: * The UV-specific endonuclease (excinuclease) recognizes bulky lesions. * It performs dual incisions on both the 5' and 3' sides of the DNA damage.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Contrast the molecular lesions addressed by Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) with those addressed by Base Excision Repair (BER).
back: * NER: Repairs bulky, helix-distorting lesions like pyrimidine dimers. * BER: Repairs small, non-bulky alterations such as deaminated bases.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Identify the inheritance pattern of Xeroderma pigmentosum and the primary environmental trigger for its clinical signs.
back: * Inheritance: Autosomal recessive. * Trigger: Exposure to non-ionizing ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: In patients with Xeroderma pigmentosum, UV radiation causes the covalent joining of adjacent [___] bases in a DNA strand.
back: * Pyrimidine (commonly Thymine). * This forms a bulky intrastrand cross-link or dimer.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: A patient with Xeroderma pigmentosum develops multiple melanomas by age 10. What is the molecular consequence of the primary repair failure?
back: * DNA polymerase cannot bypass dimers accurately. * Unrepaired lesions lead to high rates of somatic mutations and early carcinogenesis.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
front: Describe the sequence of DNA repair steps that is impaired in patients with Xeroderma pigmentosum.
back: * 1. Recognition of bulky pyrimidine dimer. * 2. Incision by UV-specific endonuclease. * 3. Excision of damaged oligonucleotide. * 4. DNA polymerase filling and ligation.

category: Interpret Xeroderma pigmentosa on basis of sign /symptoms and data
